arXiv:2507.18959v1 [math.CO] 25 Jul 2025

Higher-order Stirling cycle and subset triangles:
 Total positivity, continued fractions and real-rootedness

Bishal Deb and Alan D. Sokal Email: bishal@gonitsora.com, sokal@nyu.edu Affiliation: Yau Mathematical Sciences Center, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University College London, London WC1E 6BT, UK Affiliation: Department of Physics, New York University, New York, NY 10003, USA
July 24, 2025
Abstract

Given a lower-triangular matrix of real numbers, one can ask the following four total-positivity questions: total positivity of the triangle itself; total positivity of its row-reversal; Toeplitz-total positivity of its row sequences (equivalent to negative-real-rootedness of the row-generating polynomials); and coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity of the sequence of row-generating polynomials. In this paper, we introduce two infinite families of lower-triangular matrices generalising the Stirling cycle and subset triangles, parametrised by an integer r≥1r\geq 1; we call these the rrth-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers. We then ask the foregoing four questions for each of these triangles, leading us to several conjectures. We then prove some of these conjectures for the case r=2r=2.

Key Words: Totally positive matrix, Hankel matrix, zeros of polynomials, higher-order Stirling cycle numbers, higher-order Stirling subset numbers, Stirling permutations, increasing ternary trees, increasing ordered trees, branched continued fractions, permutations, set partitions, phylogenetic trees, log-concavity.

Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC 2020) codes: 05A15 (Primary); 05A05, 05A18, 05A19, 05A20, 11B73, 15B48, 30B70 (Secondary).

1 Introduction and statement of main results

A (finite or infinite) matrix of real numbers is called totally positive (TP) if all its minors are nonnegative. A matrix of polynomials with real coefficients is called coefficientwise totally positive if all its minors are polynomials with nonnegative coefficients. Let A=(an,k)n,k≥0A=(a_{n,k})_{n,k\geq 0} be a lower-triangular matrix of nonnegative real numbers. One can then ask the following four questions:

  1. (a)

    Is AA totally positive?

  2. (b)

    Is the lower-triangular matrix Arev=def(an,n−k)n,k≥0A^{\rm rev}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(a_{n,n-k})_{n,k\geq 0}, obtained by reversing the rows of AA, totally positive? (Here an,n−k=def0a_{n,n-k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}0 when n<kn<k.)

  3. (c)

    Let An​(x)=∑k=0nan,k​xkA_{n}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{n,k}x^{k} denote the row-generating polynomial of the nn-th row of AA. Are the polynomials An​(x)A_{n}(x) negative-real-rooted?11 1 A polynomial with real coefficients is said to be real-rooted if it is either identically zero or all its (complex) zeros are real; it is said to be negative-real-rooted if it is either identically zero or all its (complex) zeros lie in (−∞,0](-\infty,0]. Since we are here assuming that all the matrix entries an,ka_{n,k} are nonnegative, clearly An​(x)A_{n}(x) cannot have any positive real zeros unless it is identically zero. So negative-real-rootedness and real-rootedness are equivalent here. This is equivalent [33, pp. 395, 399] to asking if the Toeplitz matrix of the nn-th row sequence (an,k)k≥0(a_{n,k})_{k\geq 0} — that is, the matrix (an,i−j)i,j≥0(a_{n,i-j})_{i,j\geq 0} with an,k=def0a_{n,k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}0 for k<0k<0 — is totally positive. In this situation we say that the nn-th row sequence (an,k)k≥0(a_{n,k})_{k\geq 0} is Toeplitz-totally positive.22 2 Sequences whose Toeplitz matrices are totally positive are also known as Pólya frequency sequences. The just-cited characterisation of finitely supported Pólya frequency sequences is a special case of the (much more difficult) theorem of Aissen, Edrei, Schoenberg and Whitney [3, 20] that characterises arbitrary Pólya frequency sequences [33, p. 412, Theorem 5.3].

  4. (d)

    Is the Hankel matrix of the polynomial sequence (An​(x))n≥0(A_{n}(x))_{n\geq 0} — that is, the matrix (Ai+j​(x))i,j≥0(A_{i+j}(x))_{i,j\geq 0} — coefficientwise totally positive in the variable xx? In this situation we say that the sequence (An​(x))n≥0(A_{n}(x))_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive. One sufficient but far-from-necessary condition for this to hold is for the ordinary generating function ∑n=0∞An​(x)​tn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}A_{n}(x)t^{n} to have a Stieltjes-type continued fraction (or more generally, a Thron-type continued fraction) with coefficients that are polynomials with nonnegative coefficients in the variable xx.33 3 This result for Stieltjes-type continued fractions (S-fractions) was first stated explicitly in [41]; see [38, Theorem 9.8] for a published proof (in fact of a much more general result). However, this result is in fact an easy corollary of Flajolet’s [25] combinatorial interpretation of Stieltjes-type continued fractions together with Viennot’s [46, Chapter 4, Section 3] combinatorial characterization of the Hankel minors. The generalization to Thron-type continued fractions (T-fractions) is given (again in much greater generality) in [38, Theorem 9.9].

For several important combinatorial triangles, the answers to all four of these questions have either been proven to be yes or are conjectured to be yes. Some examples are:

  1. (a)

    When A=((nk))n,k≥0A=\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)_{n,k\geq 0} is the matrix of binomial coefficients. The binomial matrix AA is well known to be totally positive, and there are many proofs of this fact: see e.g. [2, pp. 232–233] for a proof using the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma. Here Arev=AA^{\rm rev}=A as the rows are palindromic. The row-generating polynomials An​(x)=(1+x)nA_{n}(x)=(1+x)^{n} are clearly negative-real-rooted. And finally, the sequence ((1+x)n)n≥0\big((1+x)^{n}\big)_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx: this can easily be seen directly, or it follows from the continued fraction ∑n=0∞(1+x)n​tn=1/[1−(1+x)​t]\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}(1+x)^{n}\,t^{n}=1/[1-(1+x)t].

  2. (b)

    When A=([nk])n,k≥0A=\left(\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\right)_{n,k\geq 0} is the matrix of Stirling cycle numbers, which count the permutations of [n]=def{1,…,n}[n]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\{1,\ldots,n\} with kk cycles. The total positivity of the matrix AA and its reversal ArevA^{\rm rev} are due to Brenti [8] in 1995: they hold because the entries [nk]\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k} satisfy a binomial-like recurrence with nonnegative nn-dependent coefficients. The row-generating polynomials An(x)=x(x+1)⋯(x+n−1)A_{n}(x)=x(x+1)\cdots(x+n-1) are clearly negative-real-rooted. The sequence (An​(x))n≥0\big(A_{n}(x)\big)_{n\geq 0} has a Stieltjes-type continued fraction, first discovered by Euler [24] in 1760: see e.g. [42, eqn. (1.2)] [43, eqns. (2.2)/(2.6)]. This implies the coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity.

  3. (c)

    When A=({nk})n,k≥0A=\left(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\right)_{n,k\geq 0} is the matrix of Stirling subset numbers, which count the set partitions of [n][n] with kk blocks. The total positivity of the matrix AA is due to Brenti [8] in 1995: it holds because the entries {nk}\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k} satisfy a binomial-like recurrence with nonnegative kk-dependent coefficients. However, the total positivity of the reversal ArevA^{\rm rev} was only recently shown by us in [14]. The real-rootedness of the row-generating polynomials An​(x)A_{n}(x) was proven by Harper [30] in 1967. The sequence (An​(x))n≥0\big(A_{n}(x)\big)_{n\geq 0} has a Stieltjes-type continued fraction, discovered by various people in the second half of the twentieth century: see e.g. [43, eqns. (3.2)/(3.5) and footnote 19]. This implies the coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity.

  4. (d)

    When A=(⟨nk⟩)n,k≥0A=\left(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\right)_{n,k\geq 0}, is the matrix of Eulerian numbers, which count the permutations on [n][n] with kk descents (or kk excedances). The row-generating polynomials An​(x)A_{n}(x) were shown to be real-rooted by Frobenius [26] in 1910. The sequence (An​(x))n≥0\big(A_{n}(x)\big)_{n\geq 0} has a Stieltjes-type continued fraction going back to Stieltjes [45]: see e.g. [43, eqns. (2.2)/(2.8) and footnote 4]. This implies the coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity. In 1996, Brenti [9] conjectured that the matrix AA is totally positive; this conjecture is, alas, still open.44 4 Dyachenko [18] has verified this conjecture for the leading 512×512512\times 512 submatrix of the matrix (⟨n+1k⟩)n,k≥0\left(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{k}\right)_{n,k\geq 0}, by computing the bidiagonal factorization using Neville elimination [27]. Here the rows of AA are almost-palindromic in the sense that ⟨nk⟩=⟨nn−1−k⟩\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}=\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-1-k} for n≥1n\geq 1; it easily follows from this that ArevA^{\rm rev} is totally positive if and only if AA is. In [14] we have generalized Brenti’s conjecture: we conjecture the coefficientwise total positivity of a lower-triangular matrix in six indeterminates that is defined by a particular recurrence; this matrix includes the Eulerian matrix, the Stirling subset matrix and the reversed Stirling subset matrix as special cases.

In this paper, we introduce two infinite families of lower-triangular matrices generalizing the Stirling cycle and subset triangles, parametrized by an integer r≥1r\geq 1: we call them the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order Stirling cycle and subset triangles. For r=1r=1 they reduce to the ordinary Stirling cycle and subset triangles. The central theme of this paper is to investigate the foregoing four questions for these triangular arrays. We have combined an experimental approach with proofs using both bijective and generating-function methods. Even though we are able to prove only very few of our conjectures — notably those for the case r=2r=2 — we have proven several interesting combinatorial interpretations for the rrth-order Stirling triangles, and our results suggest further interesting consequences in the form of combinatorial interpretations and additional conjectures.

The rest of this introduction is structured as follows: In Section 1.1 we define the rrth-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers and state some recurrences that these numbers satisfy; we also set up some basic notation for this paper. Then in Section 1.2 we introduce the second-order Eulerian numbers and relate them to the second-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers; this connection will play a major role in our proofs. We will also introduce two generalisations: the higher-order Eulerian numbers and the higher-order quasi-Eulerian numbers. In Section 1.3 we state our main conjectures on the higher-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers, and also state our theorems. In Section 1.4 we state some conjectures for the higher-order Eulerian and quasi-Eulerian numbers. In Section 1.5 we present the outline of the remainder of this paper.

1.1 Higher-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers

Several generalizations and extensions of the Stirling cycle and subset numbers have been introduced in the literature. One such family of generalizations are the rr-associated Stirling cycle and subset numbers, defined as follows:

The 𝒓\bm{r}-associated Stirling cycle number [nk]r\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{r} is the number of permutations on [n][n] with kk cycles, all of which are of size ≥r\geq r [16, pp. 256–257, 295]. Thus we have [nk]1=[nk]\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{1}=\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}. Note that [nk]r\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{r} is nonzero only when n≥r​kn\geq rk, or equivalently k≤⌊n/r⌋k\leq\lfloor n/r\rfloor. See [35, A132393/A106828/A050211/A050212/A050213] for 1≤r≤51\leq r\leq 5.

Similarly, the 𝒓\bm{r}-associated Stirling subset number {nk}r\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{r} is the number of set partitions of [n][n] into kk blocks, all of which are of size ≥r\geq r [16, pp. 221–222]. Thus we have {nk}1={nk}\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{1}=\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}. Note that {nk}r\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{r} is nonzero only when n≥r​kn\geq rk, or equivalently k≤⌊n/r⌋k\leq\lfloor n/r\rfloor. See [35, A048993/A008299/A059022/A059023/A059024/A059025] for 1≤r≤61\leq r\leq 6.

It is not difficult to show, by considering the possibilities for the element nn in the permutation or set partition, that the rr-associated Stirling cycle and subset numbers satisfy the recurrences [16, pp. 222, 257]

[nk]r\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{r} =\displaystyle= (r−1)!​(n−1r−1)​[n−rk−1]r+(n−1)​[n−1k]r\displaystyle(r-1)!\,\binom{n-1}{r-1}\,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-r}{k-1}_{r}\>+\>(n-1)\,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}_{r} (1.1)
{nk}r\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{r} =\displaystyle= (n−1r−1)​[n−rk−1]r+k​{n−1k}r\displaystyle\binom{n-1}{r-1}\,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-r}{k-1}_{r}\>+\>k\,\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}_{r} (1.2)

For r≥2r\geq 2, the sequences of row-generating polynomials of these triangles are not coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive. This is because the nn-th row-generating polynomial is of degree ⌊n/r⌋\lfloor n/r\rfloor — not nn — and it follows from this that even the 2×22\times 2 Hankel minors must have some negative coefficients.

Instead, we modify these triangles by shifting the columns up until we get a lower-triangular matrix with nonzero diagonal entries. That is, we define, for each r≥1r\geq 1,

[nk](r)\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)} =def\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}} [n+(r−1)​kk]r\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n+(r-1)k}{k}_{r} (1.3)
{nk}(r)\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)} =def\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}} {n+(r−1)​kk}r\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+(r-1)k}{k}_{r} (1.4)

We call these the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers, respectively; and we call the lower-triangular matrices

C(r)=def([nk](r))n,k≥0​S(r)=def({nk}(r))n,k≥0.C^{(r)}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\left(\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}\right)_{n,k\geq 0}\\ S^{(r)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\left(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}\right)_{n,k\geq 0}\;. (1.5)

the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order Stirling cycle and subset triangles. Of course we have

[nk](1)\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(1)} =\displaystyle= [nk]1=[nk]\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{1}\;=\;\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k} (1.6)
{nk}(1)\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(1)} =\displaystyle= {nk}1={nk}\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{1}\;=\;\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k} (1.7)

so that the numbers of order r=1r=1 are the usual Stirling cycle and subset numbers, respectively. For the convenience of the reader and for our use in the rest of the paper, we rewrite (1.3)/(1.4) for r=2r=2:

[nk](2)\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)} =\displaystyle= [n+kk]2\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n+k}{k}_{2} (1.8)
{nk}(2)\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)} =\displaystyle= {n+kk}2\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+k}{k}_{2} (1.9)

The triangle C(2)C^{(2)} is [35, A259456/A269940/A111999] and its row sums are [35, A032188]. The triangle S(2)S^{(2)} is [35, A134991/A269939] and its row sums are [35, A000311]. The second-order Stirling subset numbers are often referred to as the Ward numbers [47, 13, 15, 4, 23]. The row sums of C(r)C^{(r)} and S(r)S^{(r)} for r≥3r\geq 3 are not currently in the OEIS [35]. In the Appendix we provide tables of the triangles C(r)C^{(r)} and S(r)S^{(r)} for 1≤r≤41\leq r\leq 4 and the first few values of nn.

From the combinatorial definition one sees that the diagonal elements of the arrays C(r)C^{(r)} and S(r)S^{(r)} are

[nn](r)\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(r)} =\displaystyle= [r​nn]r=(r​n)!rn​n!\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{rn}{n}_{r}\;=\;{(rn)!\over r^{n}\,n!} (1.10)
{nn}(r)\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(r)} =\displaystyle= {r​nn}r=(r​n)!(r!)n​n!\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{rn}{n}_{r}\;=\;{(rn)!\over(r!)^{n}\,n!} (1.11)

[35, A001147/A052502/A060706/A052504] [35, A001147/A025035/A025036/A025037/ A025038]. In particular, for r=2r=2 we have

[nn](2)={nn}(2)=(2​n−1)!!.\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(2)}\;=\;\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(2)}\;=\;(2n-1)!!\;. (1.12)

The numbers (2​n−1)!!(2n-1)!! [10] [35, A001147] will play a central role in this paper: see Section 4.4 for an observation about this.

The recurrence relations (1.1)/(1.2) for the rr-associated Stirling cycle and subset numbers easily imply, by change of variables, the following recurrence relations for the rrth-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers:

Lemma 1.1.
  1. (a)

    The numbers [nk](r)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)} satisfy the recurrence

    [nk](r)=(r−1)!​(n+(r−1)​k−1r−1)​[n−1k−1](r)+(n+(r−1)​k−1)​[n−1k](r)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}\;=\;(r-1)!\,\binom{n+(r-1)k-1}{r-1}\,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}^{(r)}\>+\>\big(n+(r-1)k-1\big)\,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}^{(r)} (1.13)

    for n≥1n\geq 1, with initial conditions [0k](r)=δk​0\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{0}{k}^{(r)}=\delta_{k0} and [n−1](r)=0\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{-1}^{(r)}=0.

  2. (b)

    The numbers {nk}(r)\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)} satisfy the recurrence

    {nk}(r)=(n+(r−1)​k−1r−1)​{n−1k−1}(r)+k​{n−1k}(r)\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}\;=\;\binom{n+(r-1)k-1}{r-1}\,\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}^{(r)}\>+\>k\,\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}^{(r)} (1.14)

    for n≥1n\geq 1, with initial conditions {0k}(r)=δk​0\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{0}{k}^{(r)}=\delta_{k0} and {n−1}(r)=0\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{-1}^{(r)}=0.

When r=2r=2, the recurrences (1.13)/(1.14) are

[nk](2)\displaystyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)} =\displaystyle= (n+k−1)​[n−1k−1](2)+(n+k−1)​[n−1k](2)\displaystyle(n+k-1)\,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}^{(2)}\>+\>(n+k-1)\,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}^{(2)} (1.15)
{nk}(2)\displaystyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)} =\displaystyle= (n+k−1)​{n−1k−1}(2)+k​{n−1k}(2)\displaystyle(n+k-1)\,\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}^{(2)}\>+\>k\ \genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}^{(2)} (1.16)

Note that the coefficients here are affine in nn and kk (this is no longer the case for r≥3r\geq 3). It is curious that we see here the combination n+kn+k, in contrast with the n−kn-k occurring in [14, eqs. (1.2)/(1.4)/(1.5)].

We write cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x) for the row-generating polynomial of the nn-th row of the matrix C(r)C^{(r)}; we call them the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order Stirling cycle polynomials. Similarly, we write sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x) for the row-generating polynomial of the nn-th row of the matrix S(r)S^{(r)}; we call them the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order Stirling subset polynomials. Thus, we have

cr,n​(x)\displaystyle c_{r,n}(x) =def\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}} ∑k=0n[nk](r)​xk\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}x^{k} (1.17)
sr,n​(x)\displaystyle s_{r,n}(x) =def\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}} ∑k=0n{nk}(r)​xk\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}x^{k} (1.18)

Finally, we use Cwidecheck(r)\widecheck{C}^{(r)} and Swidecheck(r)\widecheck{S}^{(r)} to denote the two row-reversed matrices Cwidecheck(r)=def(C(r))rev\widecheck{C}^{(r)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\bigl(C^{(r)}\bigr)^{\rm rev} and Swidecheck(r)=def(S(r))rev\widecheck{S}^{(r)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\bigl(S^{(r)}\bigr)^{\rm rev}.

1.2 Relation with the second-order Eulerian numbers

The second-order (r=2r=2) Stirling cycle and subset numbers are closely related to the second-order Eulerian numbers, as we now explain.

Let w=w1⋯wNw=w_{1}\cdots w_{N} be a word on a totally ordered alphabet 𝔸{\mathbb{A}}. A pair (wi,wi+1)(w_{i},w_{i+1}) with i∈[N−1]i\in[N-1] is called an ascent (resp. descent, plateau) in case wi<wi+1w_{i}<w_{i+1} (resp. wi>wi+1w_{i}>w_{i+1}, wi=wi+1w_{i}=w_{i+1}).55 5 Note that we do not allow i=Ni=N as a position for an ascent, descent or plateau. Some authors do allow this, by fixing a “boundary condition” for wN+1w_{N+1} (usually defining it to be either << every element of 𝔸{\mathbb{A}} or >> every element of 𝔸{\mathbb{A}}). It is important, when comparing formulae, to check carefully which convention the author is using. The word ww is said to be a Stirling word if, for every letter a∈𝔸a\in{\mathbb{A}}, all letters between two successive occurrences of aa are larger than aa. A permutation of a multiset MM is said to be a Stirling permutation if it is a Stirling word. The second-order Eulerian number ⟨⟨nk⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle is then defined to be the number of Stirling permutations of the multiset {1,1,2,2,…,n,n}\{1,1,2,2,\ldots,n,n\} with kk ascents (or kk descents: they are equidistributed, since reversing the word exchanges ascents with descents).66 6 Here we follow the definition of Graham–Knuth–Patashnik [29, p. 270], which entails that, when n≥1n\geq 1, ⟨⟨nk⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle is nonzero for 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1. Many other authors [28, 36, 32, 19] use the convention that the final index N=2​nN=2n is always the beginning of a descent (e.g. by imposing the boundary condition wN+1=0w_{N+1}=0), so that, when n≥1n\geq 1, ⟨⟨nk⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle is nonzero for 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. They satisfy the recurrence [29, eq. (6.41)]

⟨⟨nk⟩⟩=(2​n−k−1)​⟨⟨n−1k−1⟩⟩+(k+1)​⟨⟨n−1k⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle\;=\;(2n-k-1)\,\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}\!\!\right\rangle\>+\>(k+1)\,\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}\!\!\right\rangle (1.19)

with initial conditions ⟨⟨0k⟩⟩=δk​0\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{0}{k}\!\!\right\rangle=\delta_{k0} and ⟨⟨n−1⟩⟩=0\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{-1}\!\!\right\rangle=0.

Now define the second-order Eulerian triangle E(2)=(⟨⟨nk⟩⟩)n,k≥0E^{(2)}=\big(\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle\big)_{n,k\geq 0} and the shifted-reversed second-order Eulerian triangle Ewidecheck(2)=(⟨⟨nn−k−1⟩⟩)n,k≥0\widecheck{E}^{(2)}=\big(\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-k-1}\!\!\right\rangle\big)_{n,k\geq 0} [with the modification for n=0n=0 to make the row (1,0,0,…)(1,0,0,\ldots)]. We will prove:

Proposition 1.2 (Relation of second-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers with second-order Eulerian numbers).

Let B=((nk))n,k≥0B=\big(\,\binom{n}{k}\,\big)_{n,k\geq 0} be the binomial matrix. Then:

  • (a)

    Cwidecheck(2)=E(2)​B\widecheck{C}^{(2)}\>=\>E^{(2)}\,B.

  • (b)

    Swidecheck(2)=Ewidecheck(2)​B\widecheck{S}^{(2)}\>=\>\widecheck{E}^{(2)}\,B.

Part (b) seems to have been known for a long time [40, eq. (6)] [4, eqns. (1a)/(31b)]; and part (a) is implicit in some formulas at [35, A106828/A358622]. We will give several proofs of these equalities: a simple algebraic proof based on the recurrences, which however is not very enlightening; and several (more illuminating) combinatorial proofs based on bijections to other combinatorial objects.

If one defines the second-order Eulerian polynomials

En(2)​(x)=def∑k=0n⟨⟨nk⟩⟩​xk,E^{(2)}_{n}(x)\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle x^{k}\;, (1.20)

then the identities of Proposition 1.2 imply a relation with the second-order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials:

xn​c2,n​(1/x)\displaystyle x^{n}\,c_{2,n}(1/x) =\displaystyle= En(2)​(1+x)\displaystyle E^{(2)}_{n}(1+x) (1.21)
xn​s2,n​(1/x)\displaystyle x^{n}\,s_{2,n}(1/x) =\displaystyle= (1+x)n−1​En(2)​(11+x)for n≥1\displaystyle(1+x)^{n-1}\,E^{(2)}_{n}\Big({1\over 1+x}\Big)\quad\hbox{for $n\geq 1$} (1.22)

or equivalently77 7 The identity (1.24) can also be found in [23, eq. (1.15b)]: that paper used a different definition of the second-order Eulerian numbers, so that their En[2]​(x)E^{[2]}_{n}(x) equals our x​En(2)​(x)xE^{(2)}_{n}(x) for n≥1n\geq 1.

c2,n​(x)\displaystyle c_{2,n}(x) =\displaystyle= xn​En(2)​(1+xx)\displaystyle x^{n}\,E^{(2)}_{n}\Big({1+x\over x}\Big) (1.23)
s2,n​(x)\displaystyle s_{2,n}(x) =\displaystyle= x​(1+x)n−1​En(2)​(x1+x)for n≥1\displaystyle x\,(1+x)^{n-1}\,E^{(2)}_{n}\Big({x\over 1+x}\Big)\quad\hbox{for $n\geq 1$} (1.24)

Let us remark that one can define, more generally, the rrth-order Eulerian numbers ⟨nk⟩(r)\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{\!(r)} as the number of Stirling permutations of the multiset {1r,…,nr}\{1^{r},\ldots,n^{r}\} with kk ascents. They satisfy the recurrence

⟨nk⟩(r)=[r​n−k−(r−1)]​⟨n−1k−1⟩(r)+(k+1)​⟨n−1k⟩(r).\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{\!(r)}\;=\;\big[rn-k-(r-1)\big]\,\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}^{\!(r)}\>+\>(k+1)\,\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}^{\!(r)}\;. (1.25)

We analogously define rr-th order Eulerian triangle E(r)=(⟨nk⟩(r))n,k≥0E^{(r)}=\big(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{\!(r)}\big)_{n,k\geq 0} and shifted-reversed rr-th order Eulerian triangle Ewidecheck(r)=(⟨nn−k−1⟩(r))n,k≥0\widecheck{E}^{(r)}=\big(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-k-1}^{\!(r)}\big)_{n,k\geq 0} for r≥1r\geq 1.

However, as far as we know there is no relation between the rrth-order Stirling cycle or subset numbers and the rrth-order Eulerian numbers, for r≥3r\geq 3. Indeed, this lack of relation is to be expected, since the recurrence (1.25) is affine in nn and kk for all rr, while the recurrences (1.13)/(1.14) are not affine in nn or kk when r≥3r\geq 3. Instead, the matrices which do seem to be analogous in this context for r≥3r\geq 3 are Cwidecheck(r)​B−1\widecheck{C}^{(r)}\,B^{-1} and Swidecheck(r)​B−1\widecheck{S}^{(r)}\,B^{-1}. We call their entries the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order quasi-Eulerian numbers. We will further look at these matrices in Sections 1.4 and 5: we will state some conjectures related to these numbers in Section 1.4, and we will provide a combinatorial interpretation for the entries of Cwidecheck(r)​B−1\widecheck{C}^{(r)}\,B^{-1} in Section 5.

1.3 Statement of main conjectures and results

Having defined the Stirling cycle and subset numbers of all orders rr, we are now ready to state our conjectures, which constitute our first principal contribution in this paper. We will then state which cases are known and which cases we will prove in the present paper.

Our conjecture for the Stirling cycle numbers of all orders is the following:

Conjecture 1.3 (Conjecture for Stirling cycle numbers of all orders).

The following are true:

  • (a)

    The triangle C(r)C^{(r)} is totally positive for all r≥1r\geq 1.

  • (b)

    The triangle Cwidecheck(r)=def(C(r))rev\widecheck{C}^{(r)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\left(C^{(r)}\right)^{\rm rev} formed by reversing the rows of C(r)C^{(r)} is totally positive for r=1,2r=1,2 and is not totally positive when r≥3r\geq 3.

  • (c)

    The row-generating polynomials cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x) are negative-real-rooted for r=1,2r=1,2 and they have non-real complex zeros for r≥3r\geq 3 and n≥3n\geq 3. Also, the row sequences of the matrix C(r)C^{(r)} are log-concave for 1≤r≤51\leq r\leq 5.

  • (d)

    The sequence (cr,n​(x))n≥0(c_{r,n}(x))_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx for all r≥1r\geq 1.

As mentioned earlier, the r=1r=1 cases of Conjecture 1.3 are all known to be true. In this paper we will prove (c) and (d) for r=2r=2.88 8 The log-concavity problems in (c) for r=3,4,5r=3,4,5 were proposed by the first author at the 30th British Combinatorial Conference: see [12] for the full list of problems.

Our conjecture for the Stirling subset numbers of all orders is the following:

Conjecture 1.4 (Conjecture for Stirling subset numbers of all orders).

The following are true:

  • (a)

    The triangle S(r)S^{(r)} is totally positive for all r≥1r\geq 1.

  • (b)

    The triangle Swidecheck(r)=def(S(r))rev\widecheck{S}^{(r)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\left(S^{(r)}\right)^{\rm rev} formed by reversing the rows of S(r)S^{(r)} is totally positive for r=1,2r=1,2 and is not totally positive when r≥3r\geq 3.

  • (c)

    The row-generating polynomials sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x) are negative-real-rooted for r=1,2r=1,2 and they have non-real complex zeros for r≥3r\geq 3 and n≥3n\geq 3. Also, the row sequences of the matrix S(r)S^{(r)} are log-concave for 1≤r≤51\leq r\leq 5.

  • (d)

    The sequence (sr,n​(x))n≥0(s_{r,n}(x))_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx for r=1,2r=1,2 and is not coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive for r≥3r\geq 3.

As mentioned earlier, the r=1r=1 cases of Conjecture 1.4 are all known to be true. For r=2r=2, the sequence of polynomials (s2,n​(x))n≥0(s_{2,n}(x))_{n\geq 0} was studied by Elvey Price and Sokal [23], who called them the Ward polynomials: compare the recurrence (1.16) with [23, eq. (1.6)]. They showed [23, Theorem 1.1] that these polynomials have a Thron-type continued fraction (T-fraction) with coefficients αn=n​x\alpha_{n}=nx and δn=n−1\delta_{n}=n-1. It then follows from [38, Theorem 9.9] that this sequence of polynomials is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx. Therefore, part (d) of Conjecture 1.4 is known to be true for r=2r=2. In this paper, we will prove part (c) for the case r=2r=2.

Our main result on Hankel-total positivity is therefore the following:

Theorem 1.5 (Hankel-total positivity of the second-order Stirling cycle polynomials).

The sequence of second-order Stirling cycle polynomials (c2,n​(x))n≥0(c_{2,n}(x))_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx.

This theorem is, in fact, an immediate consequence of the coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity of the second-order Eulerian polynomials [38, Corollaries 12.35 and 12.36] together with the identity (1.23). So our main work will be to prove Proposition 1.2(a): we will provide an algebraic proof (Section 2) and a combinatorial proof (Section 3). For our combinatorial proof, we need a new combinatorial interpretation for the numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}, using Stirling permutations, due to David Callan [11]; we will do this in Section 3.2.

More specifically, [38, Corollary 12.35] showed that the second-order Eulerian polynomial En(2)​(x)E^{(2)}_{n}(x) is equal to a specialization of the multivariate Eulerian polynomial 𝒫n(2)​(x0,x1,x2){\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(x_{0},x_{1},x_{2}) introduced in [38, Chapter 12]: namely, En(2)​(x)=𝒫n(2)​(1,x,x)E^{(2)}_{n}(x)={\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(1,x,x). (We will recall the precise definitions in Section 3.3.) It then follows immediately from (1.23) that the second-order Stirling cycle polynomial c2,n​(x)c_{2,n}(x) is also equal to a specialisation of the multivariate Eulerian polynomial:

c2,n​(x)=𝒫n(2)​(x,1+x,1+x).c_{2,n}(x)\;=\;{\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(x,1+x,1+x)\;. (1.26)

And from this, Theorem 1.5 follows immediately as a consequence of the coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity of the multivariate Eulerian polynomials [38, Corollary 12.3].

An analogous argument using Proposition 1.2(b) and (1.24), instead, provides an alternate proof of the coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity of the second-order Stirling subset polynomials s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x), using 2-branched S-fractions instead of classical T-fractions. This was already observed in [23, Note Added, p. 12]. The important remark here is that (1.24) gives us a way to write the second-order Stirling subset polynomials s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x) as a specialization of the multivariate Eulerian polynomials, namely,

s2,n​(x)=𝒫n(2)​(x,x,1+x).s_{2,n}(x)\;=\;{\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(x,x,1+x)\;. (1.27)

See the Remark at the end of Section 3.3.

Our second main contribution in this paper is to introduce, in Section 4, three further combinatorial interpretations for the numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}; thus, in this paper we provide a total of five combinatorial interpretations for the second-order Stirling cycle numbers. Even though these latter interpretations are not necessary for our proof of Theorem 1.5, and we are unable at present to see how to use them to prove any of our other main conjectures, we think that they are still interesting in their own right and provide interesting consequences; they also suggest new conjectures, as we will explain. We begin, in Section 4.1, by introducing our third combinatorial interpretation for the second-order Stirling cycle numbers, in terms of increasing ternary trees, using a well-known bijection to Stirling permutations. Then, in Section 4.2, we introduce our fourth interpretation in terms of certain families of weighted increasing trees with ordered children, and we provide two different proofs: one bijective and one using generating functions. Both proofs suggest new lines of investigation, and also show that the hypothesis in [37, Theorem 1.1(c)] due to Pétréolle and Sokal, though sufficient, is far from necessary. In Section 4.3 we introduce our fifth and final interpretation in terms of certain leaf-labeled trees. We then show the relation to the multivariate Ward polynomials introduced by Elvey Price and Sokal [23, pp. 9–11], and we show that these multivariate polynomials are a common generalization of both the second-order Stirling cycle polynomials c2,n​(x)c_{2,n}(x) and the second-order Stirling subset polynomials s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x). This observation leads us very naturally to another triangle of numbers that also seems to satisfy our four positivity properties; we state this in Conjecture 4.17.

Our main results on real-rootedness are the following:

Theorem 1.6 (Location of zeros for the of the second-order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials).

For each n≥1n\geq 1, the polynomials c2,n​(x)c_{2,n}(x) and s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x) have 00 as a root. The zeros of the polynomial sequence (c2,n​(x)/x)n≥1\big(c_{2,n}(x)/x\big)_{n\geq 1}, and also of the sequence (s2,n​(x)/x)n≥1\big(s_{2,n}(x)/x\big)_{n\geq 1}, are simple, interlacing, and lie in the interval (−1,0)(-1,0).

Thus, in Theorem 1.6 we prove not only that the zeros are non-positive, but that in fact they lie in a specific interval.

As mentioned previously, it is known [33, pp. 395, 399] that the Toeplitz-total positivity of the rows of a lower-triangular matrix is equivalent to the negative-real-rootedness of its row-generating polynomials. It therefore follows from Theorem 1.6 that the lower-triangular Toeplitz matrices ([ni−j](2))i,j≥0\big(\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{i-j}^{(2)}\big)_{i,j\geq 0} and ({ni−j}(2))i,j≥0\big(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{i-j}^{(2)}\big)_{i,j\geq 0} are totally positive for every n≥0n\geq 0. In particular, the positivity of the contiguous 2×22\times 2 minors of these Toeplitz matrices implies that the row sequences of the second-order Stirling cycle and subset matrices C(2)C^{(2)} and S(2)S^{(2)} are log-concave.

One can show that Theorem 1.6 follows very easily from a very general theorem due to Liu and Wang [34]. However, for the convenience of the reader we will provide a direct proof of this theorem in Section 6.

Even though the zeros of the polynomials cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x) and sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x) do not lie on the real line for r≥3r\geq 3, it might be worthwhile to try to understand how they are distributed in the complex plane. In Section 7, we will provide some plots for the distribution of zeros of the polynomials for orders r≥3r\geq 3. These plots will suggest that these zeros, when correctly normalised, seem to accumulate around some limiting curves. However, at this moment we are unable to provide any precise conjectures or proofs describing these limiting curves.

1.4 Higher-order Eulerian and quasi-Eulerian numbers: Statement of conjectures

A major longstanding open problem in the theory of total positivity is Brenti’s conjecture on the total positivity of the triangle of Eulerian numbers [9]. Brenti’s conjecture is in fact the first in a family of conjectures concerning the higher-order Eulerian numbers that arose in discussions between us and Alex Dyachenko [18]:

Conjecture 1.7 (Conjecture for rr-th order Eulerian numbers [18]).

For any r≥1r\geq 1, the following are true:

  • (a)

    The rr-th order Eulerian triangle E(r)=(⟨nk⟩(r))n,k≥0E^{(r)}=\big(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{\!(r)}\big)_{n,k\geq 0} is totally positive.

  • (b)

    The shifted-reversed rr-th order Eulerian triangle Ewidecheck(r)=(⟨nn−k−1⟩(r))n,k≥0\widecheck{E}^{(r)}=\big(\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-k-1}^{\!(r)}\big)_{n,k\geq 0} is totally positive.

We remark that (a) and (b) are equivalent for r=1r=1, by virtue of the symmetry ⟨nk⟩=⟨nn−k−1⟩\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}=\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-k-1} for n≥1n\geq 1; but this is not the case for r≥2r\geq 2, where the two conjectures need to be considered separately. Conjecture 1.7 is unproven even for r=1r=1, where it is Brenti’s conjecture from 1996 [9]. Dyachenko [18] has verified Conjecture 1.7(a,b) for the leading 512×512512\times 512 submatrix for r=1r=1, and for the leading 256×256256\times 256 submatrix for 2≤r≤62\leq r\leq 6, by computing the bidiagonal factorization using Neville elimination [27].

Conjecture 1.7 asks our questions (a) and (b) for the higher-order Eulerian triangles. Questions (c) and (d) for these triangles have already been answered in the affirmative: the negative-real-rootedness of the row-generating polynomials is due to Brenti [7, Theorem 6.6.3(i)], and their coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity was proven by Pétréolle, Sokal and Zhu [38, Corollaries 12.35 and 12.36] using branched continued fractions.

However, as mentioned previously, as far as we know there is no relation between the rrth-order Stirling cycle or subset numbers and the rrth-order Eulerian triangles E(r)E^{(r)} for r≥3r\geq 3. Rather, Proposition 1.2 suggests that the matrices that are analogous in this context for r≥3r\geq 3 are Cwidecheck(r)​B−1\widecheck{C}^{(r)}\,B^{-1} and Swidecheck(r)​B−1\widecheck{S}^{(r)}\,B^{-1}. We call these matrices the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order quasi-Eulerian cycle triangle and the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order quasi-Eulerian subset triangle, respectively, and we denote them as

QC(r)=defCwidecheck(r)​B−1,QS(r)=defSwidecheck(r)​B−1.Q_{\rm C}^{(r)}\>\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\>\widecheck{C}^{(r)}\,B^{-1},\quad Q_{\rm S}^{(r)}\>\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\>\widecheck{S}^{(r)}\,B^{-1}\;. (1.28)

We call their entries the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order quasi-Eulerian cycle numbers and the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order quasi-Eulerian subset numbers, respectively:

⟨⟨nk⟩⟩C(r)=def(QC(r))n,k,⟨⟨nk⟩⟩S(r)=def(QS(r))n,k.\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{\!(r)}_{\!\rm C}\>\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\>(Q_{\rm C}^{(r)})_{n,k},\quad\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{\!(r)}_{\!\rm S}\>\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\>(Q_{\rm S}^{(r)})_{n,k}\;. (1.29)

Thus, when r=2r=2, we have from Proposition 1.2

QC(2)=E(2),QS(2)=Ewidecheck(2),Q_{\rm C}^{(2)}\;=\;E^{(2)}\;,\qquad Q_{\rm S}^{(2)}\;=\;\widecheck{E}^{(2)}\;, (1.30)

so that the two matrices are reversals of each other. But for r≠2r\neq 2 this is not the case, and the four matrices QC(r)Q_{\rm C}^{(r)}, QS(r)Q_{\rm S}^{(r)}, (QC(r))rev\bigl(Q_{\rm C}^{(r)}\bigr)^{\rm rev}, (QS(r))rev\bigl(Q_{\rm S}^{(r)}\bigr)^{\rm rev} need to be considered separately.

In Appendices B.1 and B.2, we provide tables of the triangles QC(r)Q_{\rm C}^{(r)} and QS(r)Q_{\rm S}^{(r)}, respectively, for 1≤r≤51\leq r\leq 5 and the first few values of nn. When r=1r=1, the matrices QC(1)Q_{\rm C}^{(1)} and QS(1)Q_{\rm S}^{(1)} are not even entrywise positive: some of their entries are negative integers. We therefore restrict our discussion henceforth to r≥2r\geq 2.

For all r≥2r\geq 2, we will provide a combinatorial interpretation for the rrth-order quasi-Eulerian cycle numbers in Section 5 (Proposition 5.2). We leave it as an open problem to construct a combinatorial interpretation for the rrth-order quasi-Eulerian subset numbers.

For r=2r=2, Conjecture 1.7 asserts that the foregoing four triangles are totally positive. For r≥3r\geq 3, the triangles QC(r)Q_{\rm C}^{(r)} and QS(r)Q_{\rm S}^{(r)} are not totally positive: this is an immediate consequence of the definition (1.28) together with the failure of total positivity for the triangles Cwidecheck(r)\widecheck{C}^{(r)} and Swidecheck(r)\widecheck{S}^{(r)} that was noted in Conjectures 1.3(b) and 1.4(b) [see Appendix C]. This fact makes the following conjecture somewhat more surprising:

Conjecture 1.8 (Conjectures for the reversed higher-order quasi-Eulerian triangles).
  • (b)

    The matrix (QC(r))rev\bigl(Q_{\rm C}^{(r)}\bigr)^{\rm rev} is totally positive for all r≥2r\geq 2.

  • (b′)

    The matrix (QS(r))rev\bigl(Q_{\rm S}^{(r)}\bigr)^{\rm rev} is totally positive for all r≥2r\geq 2.

We verified the total positivity of these matrices for 3≤r≤103\leq r\leq 10 for the leading 50×5050\times 50 submatrix.

Next, for r≥2r\geq 2 we define the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order quasi-Eulerian cycle polynomials and the 𝒓𝒕​𝒉\bm{r^{th}}-order quasi-Eulerian subset polynomials to be the generating polynomials

QC,n(r)​(x)=def∑k=0n⟨⟨nk⟩⟩C(r)​xk,\displaystyle Q^{(r)}_{{\rm C},n}(x)\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{\!(r)}_{\!\rm C}x^{k}\;, (1.31)
QS,n(r)​(x)=def∑k=0n⟨⟨nk⟩⟩S(r)​xk,\displaystyle Q^{(r)}_{{\rm S},n}(x)\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{\!(r)}_{\!\rm S}x^{k}\;, (1.32)

respectively. Then by definition, we have

xn​cr,n​(1/x)=QC,n(r)​(1+x),xn​sr,n​(1/x)=QS,n(r)​(1+x),\displaystyle x^{n}c_{r,n}(1/x)\;=\;Q^{(r)}_{{\rm C},n}(1+x)\;,\qquad x^{n}s_{r,n}(1/x)\;=\;Q^{(r)}_{{\rm S},n}(1+x)\;, (1.33)

which are (1.21) and (1.22), respectively, when r=2r=2.

For r≥3r\geq 3, these polynomials are not real-rooted: that follows from (1.33) together with the non-real-rootedness of the polynomials cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x) and sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x) that was noted in Conjectures 1.3(c) and 1.4(c) [see Proposition 7.1 and Corollaries 7.2 and 7.3 and the subsequent remarks].

Likewise, it follows from (1.33) and the failure of coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity for sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x) that was noted in Conjecture 1.4(d) that the polynomials QS,n(r)​(x)Q^{(r)}_{{\rm S},n}(x) are not coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive. On the other hand, we do conjecture coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity for the quasi-Eulerian cycle polynomials:

Conjecture 1.9 (Conjectured Hankel-total positivity of the quasi-Eulerian cycle polynomials).

For all r≥3r\geq 3, the sequence (QC,n(r)​(x))n≥0(Q^{(r)}_{{\rm C},n}(x))_{n\geq 0} of the rrth-order quasi-Eulerian cycle polynomials is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx.

From (1.33) we see that Conjecture 1.9 strengthens Conjecture 1.3(d). We have tested Conjecture 1.9 up to the 9×99\times 9 Hankel matrix for 3≤r≤103\leq r\leq 10.

1.5 Structure of this paper

The plan of this paper is as follows: In Section 2 we give an algebraic proof of Proposition 1.2. In Section 3, we prove the coefficientwise Hankel-total positivity of the second-order Stirling cycle polynomials (Theorem 1.5), based on two combinatorial interprerations of the second-order Stirling cycle numbers. Then, in Section 4, we give our third, fourth and fifth combinatorial interpretations for the second-order Stirling cycle numbers; these lead to some interesting observations and another conjecture. Next, in Section 5, we generalize our second interpretation for the second-order Stirling cycle numbers to higher orders; this gives a second combinatorial interpretation for the rrth-order Stirling cycle numbers, and also for the rrth-order quasi-Eulerian cycle numbers, for all r≥2r\geq 2. After this, in Section 6, we prove Theorem 1.6 on the negative-real-rootedness of the second-order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials. Finally, in Section 7 we provide some plots for the zeros of rr-th order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials for orders r∈[3,10]r\in[3,10].

In Appendix A, we provide tables of the rrth-order Stirling cycle and subset numbers for 1≤r≤41\leq r\leq 4 and the first few values of nn; and in Appendix B, we provide tables of the rrth-order quasi-Eulerian cycle and subset numbers for 2≤r≤42\leq r\leq 4 and the first few values of nn. Then in Appendix C, we provide a report on the systematic verification of our conjectures and mention up to which order we have checked our conjectures.

2 Algebraic proof of Proposition 1.2

In this section we will prove Proposition 1.2 by using a result from [39] concerning lower-triangular arrays that satisfy a Graham–Knuth–Patashnik (GKP) recurrence.

Lemma 2.1.

[39, Corollary A.15] Let 𝐀=(A⁡(n,k))n,k≥0{\bm{A}}=\bigl(A(n,k)\bigr)_{n,k\geq 0} be a lower-triangular array defined by the GKP recurrence

A⁡(n,k)=(α​n+β​k+γ)​A​(n−1,k)+(α′​n+β′​k+γ′)​A​(n−1,k−1)A(n,k)\;=\;(\alpha n+\beta k+\gamma)\,A(n-1,k)\>+\>(\alpha^{\prime}n+\beta^{\prime}k+\gamma^{\prime})\,A(n-1,k-1) (2.1)

for n≥1n\geq 1, with initial conditions A⁡(0,k)=δk​0A(0,k)=\delta_{k0} and A⁡(n,−1)=0A(n,-1)=0. Let BξB_{\xi} be the weighted binomial matrix with entries

(Bξ)​(n,k)=(nk)​ξn−k.(B_{\xi})(n,k)\;=\;\binom{n}{k}\,\xi^{n-k}\;. (2.2)

Then the matrix product 𝐂=𝐀​Bξ{\bm{C}}={\bm{A}}\,B_{\xi} satisfies the recurrence

C⁡(n,k)\displaystyle C(n,k) =\displaystyle= [(α+ξ​α′)​n+(β+2​ξ​β′)​k+γ+ξ⁡(β′+γ′)]​C​(n−1,k)\displaystyle\bigl[(\alpha+\xi\alpha^{\prime})n\,+\,(\beta+2\xi\beta^{\prime})k\,+\,\gamma+\xi(\beta^{\prime}+\gamma^{\prime})\bigr]\,C(n-1,k) (2.3)
+(α′​n+β′​k+γ′)​C​(n−1,k−1)\displaystyle\quad+\;(\alpha^{\prime}n+\beta^{\prime}k+\gamma^{\prime})\,C(n-1,k-1)
+ξ⁡(β+ξ​β′)​(k+1)​C​(n−1,k+1)\displaystyle\quad+\;\xi\,(\beta+\xi\beta^{\prime})\,(k+1)\,C(n-1,k+1)

for n≥1n\geq 1, with initial conditions C⁡(0,k)=δk​0C(0,k)=\delta_{k0} and C⁡(n,−1)=0C(n,-1)=0.

In particular, if ξ=−β/β′\xi=-\beta/\beta^{\prime} we again obtain a recurrence of GKP form.

Proof of Proposition 1.2. (a) The recurrence (1.19) for the second-order Eulerian numbers is of GKP form with (α,β,γ,α′,β′,γ′)=(0,1,1,2,−1,−1)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime})=(0,1,1,2,-1,-1). Applying Lemma 2.1 with ξ=1\xi=1, we deduce that 𝑪=E(2)​B1{\bm{C}}=E^{(2)}\,B_{1} satisfies the GKP recurrence

C⁡(n,k)=(2​n−k−1)​C​(n−1,k)+(2​n−k−1)​C​(n−1,k−1).C(n,k)\;=\;(2n-k-1)\,C(n-1,k)\>+\>(2n-k-1)\,C(n-1,k-1)\;. (2.4)

This is exactly what is obtained from the recurrence (1.15) for the second-order Stirling cycle numbers by replacing k→n−kk\to n-k.

(b) Making the substitution k→n−k−1k\to n-k-1 in (1.19), we see that the shifted-reversed second-order Eulerian triangle Ewidecheck(2)\widecheck{E}^{(2)} satisfies a GKP recurrence with (α,β,γ,α′,β′,γ′)=(1,1,0,1,−1,0)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime})=(1,1,0,1,-1,0). Applying Lemma 2.1 with ξ=1\xi=1, we deduce that 𝑪=Ewidecheck(2)​B1{\bm{C}}=\widecheck{E}^{(2)}\,B_{1} satisfies the GKP recurrence

C⁡(n,k)=(2​n−k−1)​C​(n−1,k)+(n−k)​C​(n−1,k−1).C(n,k)\;=\;(2n-k-1)\,C(n-1,k)\>+\>(n-k)\,C(n-1,k-1)\;. (2.5)

This is exactly what is obtained from the recurrence (1.16) for the second-order Stirling subset numbers by replacing k→n−kk\to n-k. □\square

This proof is straightforward (once one has in hand Lemma 2.1), but it is not terribly illuminating. Much of the rest of this paper is therefore devoted to providing combinatorial interpretations of the second-order Stirling cycle numbers that make the identity of Proposition 1.2(a) transparent.

3 Combinatorial proof of Proposition 1.2(a)

In this section we will provide a combinatorial proof of Proposition 1.2(a). We begin by recalling the combinatorial definition of the numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)} (Section 3.1). We then proceed in Section 3.2 to establish our second combinatorial interpretation of [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}: it counts Stirling permutations of the multiset {1,1,2,2,…,n,n}\{1,1,2,2,\ldots,n,n\} with optional dots at ascents and containing n−kn-k dots. Finally, in Section 3.3, this interpretation will immediately imply Proposition 1.2(a) as a natural consequence; we obtain Theorem 1.5 as a corollary.

3.1 Interpretation I: Derangements

Let us recall that [nk](2)=[n+kk]2\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}=\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n+k}{k}_{2} is defined to be the number of permutations of [n+k][n+k] containing kk cycles, all of which are of size ≥2\geq 2. In other words, it is the number of derangements of [n+k][n+k] containing kk cycles. We write 𝒟N,k{\mathcal{D}}_{N,k} for the set of derangements of [N][N] with kk cycles. Therefore, [nk](2)=|𝒟n+k,k|\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}=|{\mathcal{D}}_{n+k,k}|. These numbers satisfy the recurrence (1.15).

3.2 Interpretation II: Stirling permutations

We will now provide a second interpretation for the numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}: they count Stirling permutations with optional dots in ascents. This interpretation can be guessed from the entries in [35, A032188], and the proof that follows is due to David Callan [11].

Let us recall that a Stirling permutation of size 𝒏\bm{n} is a permutation of the multiset {1,1,2,2,…,n,n}\{1,1,2,2,\ldots,n,n\} with the Stirling property: for every i∈[n]i\in[n], all entries between the two occurrences of ii exceed ii. Equivalently, a Stirling permutation of size nn is permutation of the multiset {1,1,2,2,…,n,n}\{1,1,2,2,\ldots,n,n\} that avoids the pattern 212212. We recall [28] that there are (2​n−1)!!(2n-1)!! Stirling permutations of size nn. An ascent-marked Stirling permutation of size 𝒏\bm{n} is now defined to be a Stirling permutation in which a dot may or may not be inserted in each ascent (we recall that an ascent is a pair ai,ai+1a_{i},a_{i+1} such that ai<ai+1a_{i}<a_{i+1}; the dot, if any, is inserted between aia_{i} and ai+1a_{i+1}). Let 𝒱n{\mathcal{V}}_{n} denote the set of ascent-marked Stirling permutations of size nn; and let 𝒱n,k{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k} denote the set of ascent-marked Stirling permutations of size nn with kk dots. Thus,

𝒱2,0={1122,1221,2211}​𝒱2,1={11⋅22,1⋅221}.{\mathcal{V}}_{2,0}&=\{1122,1221,2211\}\\ {\mathcal{V}}_{2,1}=\{11\bm{\cdot}22,1\bm{\cdot}221\}. (3.1)

Let vn,k=|𝒱n,k|v_{n,k}=\left|{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k}\right|. We will prove:

Lemma 3.1.

The numbers vn,kv_{n,k} satisfy the recurrence

vn,k=(2​n−k−1)​(vn−1,k+vn−1,k−1)v_{n,k}\;=\;(2n-k-1)\,\big(v_{n-1,k}+v_{n-1,k-1}\big) (3.2)

with initial conditions v0,k=δk​0v_{0,k}=\delta_{k0} and vn,−1=0v_{n,-1}=0. Therefore [nk](2)=vn,n−k\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}=v_{n,n-k}.

Proof [11]. Let σ∈𝒱n,k\sigma\in{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k} be an ascent-marked Stirling permutation of size nn with kk dots. Deleting the two nn’s (which are necessarily adjacent) together with the dot (if any) preceding them gives an element of 𝒱n−1,k{\mathcal{V}}_{n-1,k} if there was no dot before n​nnn, and an element of 𝒱n−1,k−1{\mathcal{V}}_{n-1,k-1} if there was a dot before n​nnn.

Conversely, to get an element σ∈𝒱n,k\sigma\in{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k} with n​nnn not preceded by a dot from a one-size-smaller ascent-marked Stirling permutation, n​nnn can be inserted into an element of 𝒱n−1,k{\mathcal{V}}_{n-1,k} in any of the 2​n−12n-1 spaces except those occupied by a dot; thus, there are 2​n−1−k2n-1-k choices. To get a σ∈𝒱n,k\sigma\in{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k} with n​nnn preceded by a dot, ⋅n​n\bm{\cdot}nn can be inserted into an element of 𝒱n−1,k−1{\mathcal{V}}_{n-1,k-1} in any of the 2​n−12n-1 spaces except the first space and those occupied by a dot; again the number of choices is 2​n−1−k2n-1-k. This proves the recurrence (3.2).

From (3.2) it follows that the numbers un,k=vn,n−ku_{n,k}=v_{n,n-k} satisfy the recurrence

un,k=(n+k−1)​(un−1,k−1+un−1,k),u_{n,k}\;=\;(n+k-1)(u_{n-1,k-1}+u_{n-1,k})\;, (3.3)

which is the same as the recurrence (1.15) satisfied by the numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}. Since these numbers also satisfy the same initial conditions, we conclude that [nk](2)=un,k\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}=u_{n,k}. □\square

3.3 Proof of Proposition 1.2(a) and Theorem 1.5

We are now ready to prove Proposition 1.2(a).

Proof of Proposition 1.2(a). To prove Proposition 1.2(a), we need to show for every n,k≥0n,k\geq 0 that

[nn−k](2)=∑i=kn⟨⟨ni⟩⟩​(ik)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-k}^{(2)}\;=\;\sum_{i=k}^{n}\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{i}\!\!\right\rangle\binom{i}{k} (3.4)

Using Lemma 3.1, we know that the left-hand side is the number of ascent-marked Stirling permutations of size nn with kk dots. This is clearly equal to the right-hand side because we can pick such an ascent-marked Stirling permutation by first picking a Stirling permutation of size nn with ii ascents (counted by ⟨⟨ni⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{i}\!\!\right\rangle) and then insert dots in kk of the ii ascents (counted by (ik)\binom{i}{k}). □\square

Theorem 1.5 will now be an immediate consequence, but we first recall some definitions and results from [38, Chapter 12]. For a fixed integer m≥1m\geq 1 and indeterminates 𝐱=(x0,x1,…,xm){\mathbf{x}}=(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}), we let 𝒬n(m)​(𝐱){\mathcal{Q}}_{n}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}}) be the generating polynomial for increasing (m+1)(m+1)-ary trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} in which each ii-edge gets a weight xix_{i}. They are homogeneous polynomials of degree nn, and symmetric under permutations of x0,…,xmx_{0},\ldots,x_{m}. We then define 𝒫n(m)​(𝐱){\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}}) by

𝒫0(m)​(𝐱)=1​𝒫n(m)​(𝐱)=x0​𝒬n−1(m)​(𝐱)for n≥1{\mathcal{P}}_{0}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}})&=1\\ {\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}})=x_{0}{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}})\qquad\hbox{for $n\geq 1$} (3.5)

Therefore, 𝒫n(m)​(𝐱){\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}}) is the generating polynomial for increasing (m+1)(m+1)-ary trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} such that the only edge (if any) emanating from the root 00 is a 00-edge and in which each ii-edge gets a weight xix_{i}. These polynomials were called the multivariate Eulerian polynomials in [38]. They are homogeneous polynomials of degree nn, and symmetric under permutations of x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}; but x0x_{0} plays a special role.

In [38, Theorem 9.8], Pétréolle, Sokal and Zhu showed that the sequence of mm-Stieltjes–Rogers polynomials Sn(m)​(𝜶)S_{n}^{(m)}({\bm{\alpha}}) (see [38, Definition 2.2] for the definition) is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the indeterminates 𝜶=(αi)i≥m{\bm{\alpha}}=(\alpha_{i})_{i\geq m}. Then in [38, eq. (12.5) and Theorem 12.1(a)] they proved that the multivariate Eulerian polynomials 𝒫n(m)​(𝐱){\mathcal{P}}^{(m)}_{n}({\mathbf{x}}) can be obtained as a specialization of the mm-Stieltjes–Rogers polynomials:

αm+j+(m+1)​k=(k+1)​xj.\alpha_{m+j+(m+1)k}\;=\;(k+1)x_{j}\;. (3.6)

Since these coefficients αi\alpha_{i} are polynomials (in fact monomials) with nonnegative coefficients in the indeterminates 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}, it follows that the sequence (𝒫n(m)​(𝐱))n≥0\big({\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}})\big)_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the indeterminates 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}. We can summarise these results as follows:

Theorem 3.2 (​​​[38, eq. (12.5) and Theorems 12.1(a) and 9.8]).

The polynomials 𝒫n(m)​(𝐱){\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}}) are equal to the mm-Stieltjes–Rogers polynomials Sn(m)​(𝛂)S_{n}^{(m)}({\bm{\alpha}}) where the weights 𝛂=(αi)i≥m{\bm{\alpha}}=(\alpha_{i})_{i\geq m} are given by

αm+j+(m+1)​k=(k+1)​xj.\alpha_{m+j+(m+1)k}\;=\;(k+1)x_{j}. (3.7)

Thus, the sequence of polynomials (𝒫n(m)​(𝐱))n≥0\big({\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(m)}({\mathbf{x}})\big)_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive with respect to the variables x0,x1,…,xmx_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}.

Proof of Theorem 1.5. The second-order Eulerian polynomial En(2)​(x)E^{(2)}_{n}(x) is equal to a specialization of the multivariate Eulerian polynomial: namely, En(2)​(x)=𝒫n(2)​(1,x,x)E^{(2)}_{n}(x)={\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(1,x,x). As the polynomials 𝒫n(2){\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)} are homogeneous in all three variables, equation (1.23), which is a consequence of Proposition 1.2(a), gives us equation (1.26). The theorem then follows from Theorem 3.2. □\square

Remark. We can now prove the analogous equation (1.27) for the second-order Stirling subset polynomials. Using (1.24) together with En(2)​(x)=𝒫n(2)​(1,x,x)E^{(2)}_{n}(x)={\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(1,x,x) and the homogeneity and symmetry of the multivariate Eulerian polynomials, we have for n≥1n\geq 1

s2,n​(x)=x​(1+x)n−1​En(2)​(x1+x)=x1+x​𝒫n(2)​(1+x,x,x)=x​𝒬n−1(2)​(1+x,x,x)=x​𝒬n−1(2)​(x,x,1+x)=𝒫n(2)​(x,x,1+x).s_{2,n}(x)&=x\,(1+x)^{n-1}\,E^{(2)}_{n}\Big({x\over 1+x}\Big)\\ ={x\over 1+x}\>{\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(1+x,x,x)\\ =x\>{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1}^{(2)}(1+x,x,x)\\ =x\>{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1}^{(2)}(x,x,1+x)\\ ={\mathcal{P}}_{n}^{(2)}(x,x,1+x)\;. (3.8)

And of course for n=0n=0 we have s2,0​(x)=𝒫0(2)​(x,x,1+x)=1s_{2,0}(x)={\mathcal{P}}_{0}^{(2)}(x,x,1+x)=1. ■\blacksquare

4 Second-order Stirling cycle numbers: Three further combinatorial interpretations

In this section we will provide three more combinatorial interpretations for the second-order Stirling cycle numbers. In Section 4.1 we provide an interpretation using increasing ternary trees. In Section 4.2 we introduce an interpretation involving increasing trees with ordered children. In Section 4.3 we introduce an interpretation involving a class of leaf-labeled trees with cyclically-ordered children.

4.1 Interpretation III: Increasing ternary trees

We begin by recalling [44, p. 573] the recursive definition of an 𝒎\bm{m}-ary tree (1≤m<∞1\leq m<\infty): it is either empty or else consists of a root together with an ordered list of mm subtrees (T0,…,Tm−1)(T_{0},\ldots,T_{m-1}), each of which is an mm-ary tree (which may be empty). We draw an edge from each vertex to the root of each of its nonempty subtrees; an edge from a vertex to the root of its iith subtree (0≤i≤m−10\leq i\leq m-1) will be called an 𝒊\bm{i}-edge. When m=2m=2, we refer to a binary tree and to its left and right edges. When m=3m=3, we refer to a ternary tree and to its left, middle and right edges.

A rooted tree on a totally ordered vertex set is called increasing if each vertex is higher-numbered than its parent; equivalently, the labels increase along each path downward from the root. It is well known [44, p. 45, Proposition 1.5.3(a)] that the number of increasing binary trees on the vertex set [n][n] is n!n!, and more generally that the number of increasing mm-ary trees on the vertex set [n][n] is the multifactorial Fn(m−1)F_{n}^{(m-1)} [5, p. 30, Example 1], where Fn(r)=def∏j=0n−1(1+j​r)F_{n}^{(r)}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+jr). In particular, the number of increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n][n] is (2​n−1)!!(2n-1)!!.

We write 𝒯n{\mathcal{T}}_{n} for the set of increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n][n]. (In particular, 𝒯0{\mathcal{T}}_{0} has a single element, namely the empty tree.) For n≥1n\geq 1, we write 𝒯n,k{\mathcal{T}}_{n,k} for the set of increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n][n] with kk left edges.

In what follows we shall also use a variant: We write 𝒯′n\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} for the set of increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} for which the only edge (if any) emanating from the root 00 is a left edge. (Thus, 𝒯′0\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{0} has a single element, namely the tree with only the root vertex 0; and in all trees T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} with n≥1n\geq 1, the root vertex 0 has a left child 1 and no other children.) We write 𝒯′n,k\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n,k} for the set of increasing ternary trees T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} that have kk left edges.

For n≥1n\geq 1, there is an obvious bijection between 𝒯n{\mathcal{T}}_{n} and 𝒯′n\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}, which also maps 𝒯n,k{\mathcal{T}}_{n,k} to 𝒯′n,k+1\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n,k+1}: namely, given T∈𝒯nT\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n} we define T′∈𝒯′nT^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} by introducing a new root vertex 0 and making TT its left subtree; and given T′∈𝒯′nT^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}, we define T∈𝒯nT\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n} by deleting the root vertex 0 and making the vertex 1 the new root. For n=0n=0, we augment this bijection by sending the empty tree T∈𝒯0,0T\in{\mathcal{T}}_{0,0} to the tree T′∈𝒯0,0T^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{T}}_{0,0} that has only the root vertex 00.

Since Stirling permutations of size nn and the set of increasing ternary trees 𝒯n{\mathcal{T}}_{n} both have cardinality (2​n−1)!!(2n-1)!!, there clearly must exist a bijection between these two sets. Indeed, such a bijection is well known [36, 32].99 9 This bijection was first mentioned by Park in [36], who attributed it to Gessel. The details of this bijection were first explicitly stated by Janson, Kuba and Panholzer in [32]. We recall this construction, and the properties that we will need, in the following lemma:

Lemma 4.1.

There is a bijection σ↦T⁡(σ)\sigma\mapsto T(\sigma) where σ\sigma is a Stirling permutations of size nn and T⁡(σ)∈𝒯nT(\sigma)\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n} is an increasing ternary tree on the vertex set [n][n]. This bijection has the property that, for each letter a∈[n]a\in[n], the first (resp. second) occurrence of the letter aa in σ\sigma is the beginning of an ascent (i.e. a=ai<ai+1a=a_{i}<a_{i+1}) if and only if the vertex aa in T⁡(σ)T(\sigma) has a middle (resp. right) child.

Proof. We begin by recalling the bijection σ↦T⁡(σ)\sigma\mapsto T(\sigma), following [32]. Let σ=a1⋯a2​n\sigma=a_{1}\cdots a_{2n} be any word on the alphabet ℤ≥1\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} such that

  • (a)

    each letter, if it occurs in σ\sigma, occurs exactly twice; and

  • (b)

    σ\sigma has the Stirling property, i.e. all entries in σ\sigma between the two occurrences of aa exceed aa.

We then recursively define a ternary tree T⁡(σ)T(\sigma) as follows:

  • •

    T⁡(σ)T(\sigma) is the empty tree if and only if σ\sigma is the empty word.

  • •

    Otherwise, let aa be the smallest letter of σ\sigma and let σ=σ0​a​σ1​a​σ2\sigma=\sigma_{0}\,a\,\sigma_{1}\,a\,\sigma_{2}. Then T⁡(σ)T(\sigma) is the ternary tree rooted at aa with T⁡(σ0)T(\sigma_{0}), T⁡(σ1)T(\sigma_{1}) and T⁡(σ2)T(\sigma_{2}) as the left, middle and right subtrees of aa, respectively.

It is easy to see that σ↦T⁡(σ)\sigma\mapsto T(\sigma) is a bijection from Stirling permutations of size nn to the set 𝒯n{\mathcal{T}}_{n} of increasing ternary trees on [n][n].

From the description of this bijection, it is clear that the first occurrence of the letter aa in σ\sigma is the first element of an ascent pair (i.e. a=ai<ai+1a=a_{i}<a_{i+1}) if and only if σ1\sigma_{1} is not the empty word, which is true if and only if the vertex labeled aa has a middle child in the ternary tree T⁡(σ)T(\sigma). Similarly, the second aa in σ\sigma is the first element of an ascent pair if and only if σ2\sigma_{2} is not the empty word, which is true if and only if the vertex labeled aa has a right child in the ternary tree T⁡(σ)T(\sigma). □\square

Thus, the ascents in σ\sigma are in correspondence with the middle and right edges of T⁡(σ)T(\sigma).

Now define an edge-marked increasing ternary tree to be an increasing ternary tree in which each middle or right edge may be marked or unmarked. (Left edges are always unmarked.) Lemma 4.1 immediately implies:

Corollary 4.2.

There is a bijection τ↦T⁡(τ)\tau\mapsto T(\tau) where τ∈𝒱n\tau\in{\mathcal{V}}_{n} is an ascent-marked Stirling permutation of size nn and T⁡(τ)T(\tau) is an edge-marked increasing ternary tree on the vertex set [n][n], such that, for each letter a∈[n]a\in[n], the first (resp. second) occurrence of the letter aa in τ\tau is followed by a dot if and only if the vertex aa in T⁡(τ)T(\tau) has a middle (resp. right) child connected by a marked edge.

Putting together Lemma 3.1 and Corollary 4.2, we conclude:

Proposition 4.3.

The number of edge-marked increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n][n] with n−kn-k marked edges (hence k−1k-1 unmarked edges) is the second-order Stirling cycle number [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}.

Now we use the bijection 𝒯n↦𝒯′n{\mathcal{T}}_{n}\mapsto\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} and to write out a different version of Proposition 4.3. First, we let 𝒯^n{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}_{n} denote the trees T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} along with optional edge markings in which each middle or right edge may be marked or unmarked. (Left edges are always unmarked.) Let 𝒯^n,k⊆𝒯^n{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}_{n,k}\subseteq{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}_{n} denote the subset of these trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} which have kk unmarked edges. We then have the following rewriting of Proposition 4.3:

Proposition 4.4.

The number of edge-marked increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} with kk marked edges — that is, |𝒯^n,k||{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}_{n,k}| — is the second-order Stirling cycle number [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}.

4.2 Interpretation IV: Increasing ordered trees

An ordered tree is a rooted tree in which the children of each vertex are linearly ordered. An increasing ordered tree is an ordered tree on a totally ordered vertex set (usually some set of integers) such that each vertex is higher-numbered than its parent; equivalently, the labels increase along each path downward from the root. It is well known [5, Corollary 1(iv)] [31] that the number of increasing ordered trees on n+1n+1 vertices is (2​n−1)!!(2n-1)!!.

A vertex in a rooted tree is called a leaf if it has no children; it is called an internal vertex (or a non-leaf) if it has at least one child.

Recall that 𝒯′n\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} denotes the set of increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} such that the only edge (if any) emanating from the root 00 is a left edge; and 𝒯′n,k\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n,k} denotes the set of trees in 𝒯′n\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} with kk left edges. Now let ℐn{\mathcal{I}}_{n} denote the set of increasing ordered trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\}, and let ℐn,k{\mathcal{I}}_{n,k} denote the set of trees in ℐn{\mathcal{I}}_{n} with kk internal vertices.1010 10 Note that when n=0n=0, the unique element of ℐ0{\mathcal{I}}_{0}, namely the tree with only the root vertex 0, belongs to ℐ0,0{\mathcal{I}}_{0,0}, because in this case the root is a leaf. We have already seen that |𝒯n′|=|ℐn|=(2n−1)!!|\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}|=|{\mathcal{I}}_{n}|=(2n-1)!!. We will refine this equality as follows:

Proposition 4.5.

The numbers |ℐn,k||{\mathcal{I}}_{n,k}| are given by

|ℐn,k|=|𝒯n,k′|=⟨⟨nn−k⟩⟩.|{\mathcal{I}}_{n,k}|\;=\;|\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n,k}|\;=\;\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-k}\!\!\right\rangle\;. (4.1)

The second equality is a direct consequence of Lemma 4.1. For the first equality, we will give two proofs: a bijective proof in Section 4.2.1, and a proof using generating functions in Section 4.2.2. Having established Proposition 4.5, we will finally be able to introduce vertex-marked increasing ordered trees in Section 4.2.3, which will be our fourth combinatorial interpretation for the numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}.

4.2.1 Bijective proof of Proposition 4.5

For n=0n=0 the claim of Proposition 4.5 is trivial, since 𝒯′0=𝒯′0,0=ℐ0=ℐ0,0\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{0}=\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{0,0}={\mathcal{I}}_{0}={\mathcal{I}}_{0,0} has a unique element, namely the tree consisting only of the root vertex 0. So from now on we fix n≥1n\geq 1.

We will prove Proposition 4.5 by constructing a bijection Φn:𝒯′n→ℐn\Phi_{n}\colon\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}\to{\mathcal{I}}_{n} that maps 𝒯′n,k\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n,k} onto ℐn,k{\mathcal{I}}_{n,k}. We will first construct the map Φn:𝒯′n→ℐn\Phi_{n}\colon\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}\to{\mathcal{I}}_{n}; we will then construct another map Ψn:ℐn→𝒯′n\Psi_{n}\colon{\mathcal{I}}_{n}\to\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}; finally, we will show that the maps Φn\Phi_{n} and Ψn\Psi_{n} are inverses of each other. Before doing all this, we first introduce some terminology concerning trees T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} and S∈ℐnS\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}.

Let T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} and let j∈[n]∪{0}j\in[n]\cup\{0\} be a vertex of TT. Consider the subtree of TT rooted at the vertex jj that uses all the middle and right edges but no left edge. We call this tree the middle-right subtree of 𝒋\bm{j} in 𝑻\bm{T}.

Now let ii be a vertex of TT. If ii has a left child jj, we define 𝐥𝐞𝐟𝐭(𝒊)𝑻{\bf left}\bm{{}_{T}(i)} to be the middle-right subtree of jj in TT; if ii has no left child, we define leftT​(i){\rm left}_{T}(i) to be the empty tree. For example, in Figure 1(a), the tree leftT​(1){\rm left}_{T}(1) is the subtree consisting of the vertex 33, the tree leftT​(2){\rm left}_{T}(2) is the subtree induced by the vertices 4,84,8 and 99, and the tree leftT​(4){\rm left}_{T}(4) is the empty tree.

Now let jj be any vertex of TT other than the root, and consider the unique path in TT from jj to the root 0. Clearly this path must contain at least one left edge, since the root has only a left edge. Let lanc⁡(j){\rm lanc}(j) be the first vertex on this path that is reached via a left edge; we refer to lanc⁡(j){\rm lanc}(j) as the left ancestor of jj. Since the tree TT is increasing, we have 0≤lanc⁡(j)<j0\leq{\rm lanc}(j)<j. For example, in Figure 1(a), lanc⁡(1)=0{\rm lanc}(1)=0, lanc⁡(2)=0{\rm lanc}(2)=0 and lanc⁡(3)=1{\rm lanc}(3)=1.

The following lemma is a direct consequence of the definitions of leftT​(i){\rm left}_{T}(i) and lanc⁡(j){\rm lanc}(j) and we state it without proof:

Lemma 4.6.

Let T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} and let jj be a vertex of TT different from the root 00. Then jj is a vertex of leftT​(lanc​(j)){\rm left}_{T}({\rm lanc}(j)) and for every i≠lanc⁡(j)i\neq{\rm lanc}(j), jj is not a vertex of leftT​(i){\rm left}_{T}(i).

Next, let S∈ℐnS\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n} and let i∈[n]∪{0}i\in[n]\cup\{0\} be a vertex of SS. Then we define the child word of 𝒊\bm{i}, denoted by chS​(i){\rm ch}_{S}(i), to be the word whose jj-th letter is the jj-th child of ii. Thus, chS​(i){\rm ch}_{S}(i) is the empty word when ii is a leaf. For example, in Figure 1(b), we have chS​(1)=3{\rm ch}_{S}(1)=3, chS​(2)=849{\rm ch}_{S}(2)=849, and chS​(4)=∅{\rm ch}_{S}(4)=\varnothing.

We need one more ingredient before describing the map Φn\Phi_{n}. This is the well-known correspondence between increasing binary trees on a totally-ordered finite vertex set AA, and words ww on the alphabet AA with no repeated letters: see e.g. [44, pp. 44–45]. However, in our version, instead of using binary trees with left and right edges, we will use ternary trees with middle and right edges but no left edges; the two formulations are of course isomorphic. The correspondence therefore goes as follows:

If the word w=∅w=\varnothing, then Tree⁡(w)=∅{\rm Tree}(w)=\varnothing. Otherwise, write w=u⋅i⋅vw=u\cdot i\cdot v where ii is the smallest letter of ww; we then recursively define Tree⁡(w){\rm Tree}(w) to be the ternary tree with root ii whose middle subtree is Tree⁡(u){\rm Tree}(u) and right subtree is Tree⁡(v){\rm Tree}(v).

On the other hand, given an increasing ternary tree TT on the vertex set AA made up solely of middle and right edges, we define Word⁡(T){\rm Word}(T) as follows: If T=∅T=\varnothing, then Word⁡(T)=∅{\rm Word}(T)=\varnothing. Otherwise, if TT has root ii with middle subtree T′T^{\prime} and right subtree T′′T^{\prime\prime} (either or both of which may be empty), we define Word⁡(T)=Word⁡(T′)⋅i⋅Word⁡(T′′){\rm Word}(T)={\rm Word}(T^{\prime})\cdot i\cdot{\rm Word}(T^{\prime\prime}).

From the construction of the maps w↦Tree⁡(w)w\mapsto{\rm Tree}(w) and T↦Word⁡(T)T\mapsto{\rm Word}(T), we clearly have:

Lemma 4.7.
  • (a)

    Let ww be a word on the alphabet AA with no repeated letters. Then
    w=Word⁡(Tree⁡(w))w={\rm Word}({\rm Tree}(w)).

  • (b)

    Let TT be an increasing ternary tree on the vertex set AA, made up solely of middle and right edges. Then T=Tree⁡(Word⁡(T))T={\rm Tree}({\rm Word}(T)).

Construction of the map Φ𝒏:𝒯′𝒏→ℐ𝒏\bm{\Phi_{n}:\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}\to{\mathcal{I}}_{n}}.
Given a tree T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}, we will now construct a tree Φn​(T)∈ℐn\Phi_{n}(T)\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}. To do this, we begin with a tree containing only the root vertex 0. We then iterate jj from 00 through nn and insert the children of jj in Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T) as follows: We consider the subtree leftT​(j){\rm left}_{T}(j) in TT; it consists solely of middle and right edges. The children of jj in Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T) are then defined to be the letters of Word​(leftT​(j)){\rm Word}\big({\rm left}_{T}(j)\big), which are inserted in order from left to right. That is,

chΦn​(T)​(j)=Word⁡(leftT​(j)).{\rm ch}_{\Phi_{n}(T)}(j)\;=\;{\rm Word}\big({\rm left}_{T}(j)\big)\;. (4.2)

This defines an ordered tree Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T) on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\}. See Figure 1 for an example of a tree T∈𝒯′10T\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{10} and Φ10​(T)∈ℐ10\Phi_{10}(T)\in{\mathcal{I}}_{10}.

To show that Φn​(T)∈ℐn\Phi_{n}(T)\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}, we need to show that the tree Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T) is increasing, i.e. that every vertex j∈[1,n]j\in[1,n] has a parent in Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T) with label strictly smaller than jj. We do this by identifying the parent as follows:

Lemma 4.8.

Let j∈[1,n]j\in[1,n] be a non-root vertex in TT, and let lanc⁡(j){\rm lanc}(j) be its left ancestor. Then lanc⁡(j){\rm lanc}(j) is the parent of jj in Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T).

Proof. Let ii be the parent of jj in Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T). Then, jj is a letter in the child word chΦn​(T)​(i){\rm ch}_{\Phi_{n}(T)}(i). From (4.2), jj must be a vertex of leftT​(i).{\rm left}_{T}(i). Thus, from Lemma 4.6 it follows that i=lanc⁡(j)i={\rm lanc}(j). □\square

Since lanc⁡(j)<j{\rm lanc}(j)<j, we have shown:

Corollary 4.9.

For T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}, we have Φn​(T)∈ℐn\Phi_{n}(T)\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}.

Construction of the map Ψn:ℐn→𝒯′n\Psi_{n}:{\mathcal{I}}_{n}\to\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}.
Given a tree S∈ℐnS\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}, we will now construct a tree Ψn(S)∈𝒯n′\Psi_{n}(S)\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} as follows: We start with a tree rooted at 00. We then iterate through i∈[n]∪{0}i\in[n]\cup\{0\} and look at chS​(i){\rm ch}_{S}(i), the child word of ii in SS. If chS​(i)=∅{\rm ch}_{S}(i)=\varnothing, then ii will have no left child in Ψn​(S)\Psi_{n}(S). Otherwise, we create a left edge emanating from ii in Ψn​(S)\Psi_{n}(S) and attach to it the ternary tree Tree​(chS​(i)){\rm Tree}\big({\rm ch}_{S}(i)\big) consisting solely of middle and right edges. Thus, we have

leftΨn​(S)​(i)=Tree⁡(chS​(i)).{\rm left}_{\Psi_{n}(S)}(i)\;=\;{\rm Tree}\big({\rm ch}_{S}(i)\big)\;. (4.3)

When n=0n=0, we clearly have Ψ0(S)∈𝒯0′\Psi_{0}(S)\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{0}. For n≥1n\geq 1, we will now show that Ψn(S)∈𝒯n′\Psi_{n}(S)\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}. In the construction of Ψn​(S)\Psi_{n}(S), a vertex ii gets a left child jj only when chS​(i)≠∅{\rm ch}_{S}(i)\neq\varnothing and when jj is the root of Tree​(chS​(i)){\rm Tree}\big({\rm ch}_{S}(i)\big), or in other words jj is the smallest letter in chS​(i){\rm ch}_{S}(i) which is the same as saying that jj is the smallest-numbered child of the vertex ii in SS. Thus, it is clear that every vertex ii in Ψn​(S)\Psi_{n}(S) can contain at most one left child jj and that j>ij>i. Next, notice that a vertex ii in Ψn​(S)\Psi_{n}(S) gets a middle (resp. right) child jj only if ii and jj are both letters of the child word chS​(i♭){\rm ch}_{S}\big(i^{\flat}\big), for some vertex i♭i^{\flat} in TT, and jj is the middle (resp. right) child of ii in Tree⁡(chS​(i♭)){\rm Tree}\big({\rm ch}_{S}\big(i^{\flat}\big)\big). Thus, it is clear that every vertex ii in Ψn​(S)\Psi_{n}(S) can contain at most one middle child jj and at most one right child jj; furthermore, j>ij>i since Tree⁡(chS​(i♭)){\rm Tree}\big({\rm ch}_{S}\big(i^{\flat}\big)\big) is an increasing tree. Also, 00 cannot have any middle or right children in Ψn​(S)\Psi_{n}(S) as it does not have any siblings in SS. This shows that:

Lemma 4.10.

Given S∈ℐnS\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}, we have Ψn(T)∈𝒯n′\Psi_{n}(T)\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}.

We are now ready to prove Proposition 4.5.

Proof of Proposition 4.5 using bijection. We will first show that the maps Φn\Phi_{n} and Ψn\Psi_{n} are inverses of each other. Then we will argue that the number of left edges of a tree T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} equals the number of internal vertices of the tree Φn​(T)∈ℐn\Phi_{n}(T)\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}.

From equations (4.2) and (4.3) and Lemma 4.7, we observe the following:

  • (a)

    For a tree T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} and a vertex j∈[n]∪{0}j\in[n]\cup\{0\} of TT, we have

    leftΨn​(Φn​(T))​(j)=Tree⁡(chΦn​(T)​(j))=Tree⁡(Word⁡(leftT​(j)))=leftT​(j).{\rm left}_{\Psi_{n}(\Phi_{n}(T))}(j)&={\rm Tree}({{\rm ch}_{\Phi_{n}(T)}(j)})\\ ={\rm Tree}({\rm Word}({\rm left}_{T}(j)))\\ ={\rm left}_{T}(j)\;. (4.4)

    Thus, for the trees T,Ψn​(Φn​(T))T,\Psi_{n}(\Phi_{n}(T)) every vertex j∈[n]∪{0}j\in[n]\cup\{0\} satisfies
    leftΨn​(Φn​(T))​(j)=leftT​(j){\rm left}_{\Psi_{n}(\Phi_{n}(T))}(j)={\rm left}_{T}(j). We now need the following lemma:

    Lemma 4.11.

    Let T1,T2∈𝒯′nT_{1},T_{2}\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}. If leftT1​(j)=leftT2​(j){\rm left}_{T_{1}}(j)={\rm left}_{T_{2}}(j) for all j∈[n]∪{0}j\in[n]\cup\{0\}, then T1=T2T_{1}=T_{2}.

    Proof. From Lemma 4.6, recall that every vertex i≠0i\neq 0 belongs to exactly one of the subtrees leftT1​(j){\rm left}_{T_{1}}(j) (resp. leftT2​(j){\rm left}_{T_{2}}(j)) in tree T1T_{1} (resp. T2T_{2}). Since leftT1​(j)=leftT2​(j){\rm left}_{T_{1}}(j)={\rm left}_{T_{2}}(j), a vertex ii is the middle (resp. right) child of a vertex i♭i^{\flat} in tree T1T_{1} if and only if ii is the middle (resp. right) child of i♭i^{\flat} in tree T2T_{2}. Also, a vertex ii is the left child of a vertex i♭i^{\flat} in tree T1T_{1} (resp. T2T_{2}) if and only if it is the root of the tree leftT1​(i♭){\rm left}_{T_{1}}(i^{\flat}) (resp. leftT2​(i♭){\rm left}_{T_{2}}(i^{\flat})). Thus, we also get that ii is the left child of i♭i^{\flat} in tree T1T_{1} if and only if ii is the left child of i♭i^{\flat} in tree T2T_{2}. Thus, T1=T2T_{1}=T_{2}. □\square

    Lemma 4.11 and equation (4.4) together imply Ψn​(Φn​(T))=T\Psi_{n}(\Phi_{n}(T))=T.

  • (b)

    For a tree S∈ℐnS\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n} and a vertex i∈[n]∪{0}i\in[n]\cup\{0\} of SS, we have

    chΦn​(Ψn​(S))​(i)=Word⁡(leftΨn​(S)​(i))=Word⁡(Tree⁡(chS​(i)))=chS​(i){\rm ch}_{\Phi_{n}(\Psi_{n}(S))}(i)&={\rm Word}({\rm left}_{\Psi_{n}(S)}(i))\\ ={\rm Word}({\rm Tree}({\rm ch}_{S}(i)))\\ ={\rm ch}_{S}(i) (4.5)

    Equation (4.5) gives us Φn​(Ψn​(S))=S\Phi_{n}(\Psi_{n}(S))=S.

Thus, Φn\Phi_{n} and Ψn\Psi_{n} are inverses of each other.

Finally, notice that a vertex jj has a left edge in T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} if and only if jj has a non-empty child word in the tree Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T), which is true if and only if ii is an internal vertex of Φn​(T)\Phi_{n}(T). Thus, we have |𝒯′n,k|=|ℐn,k||\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n,k}|=|{\mathcal{I}}_{n,k}|. □\square

Remark. A different bijection between increasing ternary trees and increasing ordered trees was given by Janson, Kuba and Panholzer [32]. Our bijection is new and is different from theirs. We thank Markus Kuba for his comments on this. ■\blacksquare

4.2.2 Generating-function proof of Proposition 4.5
