We will now use generating functions to provide an alternate proof of Proposition 4.5; this approach also situates it as a special case of a more general result, to be enunciated in Proposition 4.12. We begin by introducing a framework for enumerating increasing ordered trees with very general vertex weights, which was first introduced by Bergeron, Flajolet and Salvy [5] and was further applied in [37].

Let ϕ=(ϕi)i≥0{\bm{\phi}}=(\phi_{i})_{i\geq 0} be indeterminates, and consider increasing ordered trees on nn vertices (here we will use the labels 0,…,n−10,\ldots,n-1) in which each vertex with ii children gets a weight ϕi\phi_{i}; the weight of the tree, denoted wt⁡(T){\rm wt}(T), is the product of the weights of its vertices. Let F⁡(t,ϕ)F(t;{\bm{\phi}}) be the weighted exponential generating function of such trees, not including the empty tree:

F⁡(t,ϕ)=def∑n=1∞(∑S∈ℐn−1wt⁡(S))​tnn!.F(t;{\bm{\phi}})\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n-1}}{\rm wt}(S)\right)\dfrac{t^{n}}{n!}\;. (4.6)

Also let Φ⁡(u)\Phi(u) be the ordinary generating function of ϕ{\bm{\phi}}:

Φ⁡(u)=def∑n=0∞ϕi​ui.\Phi(u)\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\phi_{i}u^{i}\;. (4.7)

We call Φ⁡(u)\Phi(u) the degree function. It is not difficult to show, by classifying trees according to the degree of the root, that F⁡(t,ϕ)F(t;{\bm{\phi}}) satisfies the differential equation [5, eq. (8)]

dd​t​F​(t,ϕ)=Φ⁡(F⁡(t,ϕ)).\dfrac{d}{dt}F(t;{\bm{\phi}})\;=\;\Phi(F(t;{\bm{\phi}}))\;. (4.8)

Notice that even though we defined the generating function F⁡(t,ϕ)F(t;{\bm{\phi}}) using increasing ordered trees, this set-up is very general and we can use different degree functions to enumerate different families of weighted trees. For example, if we substitute ϕi=ϕ~i/i!\phi_{i}=\widetilde{\phi}_{i}/i!, we may think of F⁡(t,ϕ)F(t;{\bm{\phi}}) as the exponential generating function enumerating increasing unordered trees where each vertex with ii children gets weight ϕ~i\widetilde{\phi}_{i}.

It turns out that the connection between increasing ternary trees and increasing ordered trees that is asserted in Proposition 4.5 is a special case of a more general connection between increasing trees with degree functions Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi that are related in a particular way, as follows:

Proposition 4.12.

Let Φ^​(u)\widehat{\Phi}(u) be a formal power series with zero constant term, and let 𝒳⁡(s){\mathcal{X}}(s) be a formal power series satisfying

Φ^′​(u)=𝒳⁡(Φ^​(u)).\widehat{\Phi}^{\prime}(u)\;=\;{\mathcal{X}}(\widehat{\Phi}(u))\;. (4.9)

Now define

Φ⁡(u)=def1+x​Φ^​(u)​Ψ​(u)=def(1+x​u)​𝒳​(u)\Phi(u)&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}1\,+\,x\>\widehat{\Phi}(u){}\\ \Psi(u)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(1\,+\,xu)\>{\mathcal{X}}(u){} (4.10)

Let 𝒜⁡(t)=defF⁡(t,ϕ){\mathcal{A}}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}F(t;{\bm{\phi}}) with degree function Φ⁡(u)\Phi(u), and let ℬ⁡(t)=defF⁡(t,𝛙){\mathcal{B}}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}F(t;{\bm{\psi}}) with degree function Ψ⁡(u)\Psi(u). Then the following identities hold:

ℬ⁡(t)=Φ^​(𝒜⁡(t))​𝒜′​(t)=1+x​ℬ​(t){\mathcal{B}}(t)&=\widehat{\Phi}({\mathcal{A}}(t)){}\\ {\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}(t)=1+x{\mathcal{B}}(t){} (4.11)

Proof. The definition ℬ⁡(t)=F⁡(t,𝝍){\mathcal{B}}(t)=F(t;{\bm{\psi}}) implies the differential equation

ℬ′​(t)=Ψ⁡(ℬ⁡(t))=(1+x​ℬ​(t))​𝒳​(ℬ⁡(t)){\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}(t)\;=\;\Psi({\mathcal{B}}(t))\;=\;(1\,+\,x{\mathcal{B}}(t))\>{\mathcal{X}}({\mathcal{B}}(t)) (4.12)

by (4.8) and (). On the other hand, the definition 𝒜⁡(t)=F⁡(t,ϕ){\mathcal{A}}(t)=F(t;{\bm{\phi}}) implies the differential equation

dd​t​Φ^​(𝒜⁡(t))=Φ^′​(𝒜⁡(t))​𝒜′​(t)=𝒳⁡(Φ^​(𝒜⁡(t)))​Φ​(𝒜⁡(t))=𝒳⁡(Φ^​(𝒜⁡(t)))​[1+x​Φ^​(𝒜⁡(t))]\dfrac{d}{dt}\widehat{\Phi}({\mathcal{A}}(t))&=\widehat{\Phi}^{\prime}({\mathcal{A}}(t))\>{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}(t)\\ ={\mathcal{X}}(\widehat{\Phi}({\mathcal{A}}(t)))\>\Phi({\mathcal{A}}(t))\\ ={\mathcal{X}}(\widehat{\Phi}({\mathcal{A}}(t)))\>\big[1+x\widehat{\Phi}({\mathcal{A}}(t))\big] (4.13)

by the chain rule, (4.9), (4.8) and (). So ℬ⁡(t){\mathcal{B}}(t) and Φ^​(𝒜​(t))\widehat{\Phi}({\mathcal{A}}(t)) satisfy the same differential equation with the same initial condition (namely, they vanish at t=0t=0), hence they are equal. This proves ().

Then

𝒜′​(t)=Φ⁡(𝒜⁡(t))= 1+x​Φ^​(𝒜⁡(t))= 1+x​ℬ​(t){\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}(t)\;=\;\Phi({\mathcal{A}}(t))\;=\;1+x\widehat{\Phi}({\mathcal{A}}(t))\;=\;1+x{\mathcal{B}}(t) (4.14)

by (4.8), () and (). This proves (). □\square

Proof of Proposition 4.5 using generating functions. We will now prove Proposition 4.5 by using Proposition 4.12. First, consider the exponential generating function OPEN𝒜⁡(t)=defF​(t,(δi​0+(1−δi​0)​x​yi−1))i≥0){\mathcal{A}}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}F\big(t;(\delta_{i0}+(1-\delta_{i0})xy^{i-1}))_{i\geq 0}\big): thus, 𝒜⁡(t){\mathcal{A}}(t) is the exponential generating function for increasing ordered trees on nn labeled vertices where each leaf is given weight ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1 and each vertex with i≥1i\geq 1 children is given weight ϕi=x​yi−1\phi_{i}=xy^{i-1}. Therefore, the degree function is

Φ⁡(u)= 1+x​u1−y​u\Phi(u)\;=\;1\,+\,\dfrac{xu}{1-yu}\; (4.15)

and 𝒜⁡(t){\mathcal{A}}(t) satisfies the differential equation

𝒜′= 1+x​𝒜1−y​𝒜.{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}\;=\;1+\dfrac{x{\mathcal{A}}}{1-y{\mathcal{A}}}\;. (4.16)

In the weight ϕi=(x/y)​yi\phi_{i}=(x/y)y^{i} for internal vertices, we can transfer a weight yy to each of the ii children; since every vertex other than the root is a child, we end up with a weight yy for leaves and xx for internal vertices, with an overall factor 1/y1/y because the root is not a child. Therefore, from (4.6) we have

𝒜⁡(t)=∑n=1∞(∑S∈ℐn−1xintvertex⁡(S)​yleaf⁡(S)−1)​tnn!{\mathcal{A}}(t)\;=\;\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n-1}}x^{{\rm intvertex}(S)}y^{{\rm leaf}(S)-1}\right)\dfrac{t^{n}}{n!} (4.17)

where intvertex⁡(S){\rm intvertex}(S) and leaf⁡(S){\rm leaf}(S) denote the number of internal vertices and leaves of of the tree S∈ℐn−1S\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n-1}, respectively.

We use the notation from Proposition 4.12 to obtain

Φ^​(u)=u1−y​u​𝒳​(s)=(1+y​s)2​Ψ​(u)=(1+x​u)​(1+y​u)2\widehat{\Phi}(u)&=\dfrac{u}{1-yu}\\ {\mathcal{X}}(s)=(1+ys)^{2}\\ \Psi(u)=(1+xu)(1+yu)^{2} (4.18)

We then define ℬ⁡(t)=defF⁡(t,𝝍){\mathcal{B}}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}F(t;{\bm{\psi}}) with degree function Ψ⁡(u)=(1+x​u)​(1+y​u)2\Psi(u)=(1+xu)(1+yu)^{2}. We can interpret ℬ⁡(t){\mathcal{B}}(t) as the exponential generating function for increasing ternary trees on the vertex set [n][n], where each left edge gets a weight xx and each middle or right edge gets a weight yy, and the weight of a tree is the product of the weights of its edges. Passing to trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} in which the only edge (if any) emanating from the root is a left edge, we get an exponential generating function

1+xℬ(t)=∑n=0∞(∑T∈𝒯′nxl⁡(T)ym⁡(T)+r⁡(T))tnn!1+x\,{\mathcal{B}}(t)\;=\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{T\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}}x^{{\rm l}(T)}y^{{\rm m}(T)+{\rm r}(T)}\right)\dfrac{t^{n}}{n!} (4.19)

where l⁡(T),m⁡(T),r⁡(T){\rm l}(T),{\rm m}(T),{\rm r}(T) denote the number of left, middle and right edges of a tree T∈𝒯nT\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n}, respectively. Finally, we use Proposition 4.12 to obtain

𝒜′​(t)= 1+x​ℬ​(t){\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}(t)\;=\;1+x\,{\mathcal{B}}(t) (4.20)

Combining equations (4.17), (4.19) and (4.20) finishes the proof. □\square

We end this section with a few remarks concerning some interesting special cases of Proposition 4.12:

Remarks. 1. If we take 𝒳⁡(s)=1+y​s{\mathcal{X}}(s)=1+ys and solve (4.9), we get Φ^​(u)=(ey​u−1)/y\widehat{\Phi}(u)\;=\;(e^{yu}-1)/y and hence

Φ⁡(u)= 1+xy​(ey​u−1),\Phi(u)\;=\;1\>+\>{x\over y}\,(e^{yu}-1)\;, (4.21)

so that ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1 and ϕi=x​yi−1/i!\phi_{i}=xy^{i-1}/i! for i≥1i\geq 1. It follows that 𝒜⁡(t){\mathcal{A}}(t) is the exponential generating function for increasing unordered trees on the vertex set [n−1]∪{0}[n-1]\cup\{0\}, with a weight 1 for each leaf and a weight x​yi−1xy^{i-1} for each vertex with i≥1i\geq 1 children; or equivalently (as we saw in the foregoing proof), with a weight yy for leaves and xx for internal vertices and an overall factor 1/y1/y. On the other hand,

Ψ⁡(u)=(1+x​u)​(1+y​u),\Psi(u)\;=\;(1+xu)(1+yu)\;, (4.22)

so that ℬ⁡(t){\mathcal{B}}(t) is the exponential generating function for increasing binary trees trees on the vertex set [n][n], with a weight xx for each left edge and yy for each right edge. Specializing to x=y=1x=y=1, this shows

ℬ⁡(t)|x=y=1=exp⁡(𝒜⁡(t)|x=y=1)−1=𝒜′​(t)|x=y=1−1,{\mathcal{B}}(t)|_{x=y=1}\;=\;\exp({\mathcal{A}}(t)|_{x=y=1})-1\;=\;{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}(t)|_{x=y=1}-1, (4.23)

i.e., unordered increasing trees on n+1n+1 vertices are equinumerous with increasing binary trees on nn vertices, a fact that is well known and can be proven bijectively [44, pp. 44–46]. Furthermore, this also tells us that the left edges in the binary trees are in correspondence with the internal vertices in the corresponding unordered increasing tree.

2. If we take 𝒳⁡(s)=(1+y​s)k{\mathcal{X}}(s)=(1+ys)^{k} with k≠1k\neq 1 and solve (4.9), we obtain

Φ^​(u)=[1−(k−1)yu]−1/(k−1)−1y.\widehat{\Phi}(u)\;=\;\dfrac{[1-(k-1)yu]^{-1/(k-1)}-1}{y}\;. (4.24)

In particular, for integer k≥2k\geq 2, the degree function Φ⁡(u)=1+x​Φ^​(u)\Phi(u)=1+x\widehat{\Phi}(u) obtained from (4.24) describes increasing ordered trees in which each leaf gets a weight ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1 and each vertex with i≥1i\geq 1 children gets a weight ϕi=1i!​x​yi−1​∏j=1i−1[1+j⁡(k−1)]\phi_{i}=\dfrac{1}{i!}xy^{i-1}\prod\limits_{j=1}^{i-1}[1+j(k-1)] (in particular, ϕ1=x\phi_{1}=x). When k=2k=2 this reduces to the situation addressed in Proposition 4.5 [cf. (4.18)]. Such trees on n+1n+1 vertices are in bijection with (k+1)(k+1)-ary trees on n+1n+1 vertices in which the root can have only a first child.

3. If we take 𝒳⁡(s)=ey​s{\mathcal{X}}(s)=e^{ys} and solve (4.9), we obtain

Φ^​(u)=−1y​log⁡(1−y​u)\widehat{\Phi}(u)\;=\;-\,{1\over y}\,\log(1-yu) (4.25)

and hence

Φ⁡(u)= 1−xy​log⁡(1−y​u),\Phi(u)\;=\;1\>-\,{x\over y}\,\log(1-yu)\;, (4.26)

so that ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1 and ϕi=x​yi−1/i\phi_{i}=xy^{i-1}/i for i≥1i\geq 1. It follows that 𝒜⁡(t){\mathcal{A}}(t) is the exponential generating function for increasing cyclically-ordered trees on the vertex set {0}∪[n−1]\{0\}\cup[n-1], with a weight 1 for each leaf and a weight x​yi−1xy^{i-1} for each vertex with i≥1i\geq 1 children; or equivalently, with a weight yy for leaves and xx for internal vertices and an overall factor 1/y1/y. On the other hand,

Ψ⁡(u)=(1+x​u)​ey​u,\Psi(u)\;=\;(1+xu)\,e^{yu}\;, (4.27)

so that ℬ⁡(t){\mathcal{B}}(t) is the exponential generating function for increasing trees on vertex set [n][n] in which every vertex has zero or one left child (with weight xx) and an arbitrary number of unordered right children (with weight yy). Therefore, 1+x​ℬ​(t)1+x{\mathcal{B}}(t) is the exponential generating function for increasing trees of the same type on vertex set {0}∪[n]\{0\}\cup[n], but in which the root 00 can only have a left child. It follows that these trees are in bijection with cyclically-ordered trees on the vertex set {0}∪[n]\{0\}\cup[n].

Problem 4.13.

Find bijections that explain Remarks 2 and 3.

4. On specializing to y=1+xy=1+x in the degree function (4.15), we obtain the weights ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1 and ϕi=x​(1+x)i−1\phi_{i}=x(1+x)^{i-1} for i≥1i\geq 1. This sequence is not coefficientwise Toeplitz-totally positive in the variable xx — or even Toeplitz-totally positive for any fixed real number x>0x>0 — since its generating function

Φ⁡(u)= 1+∑i=1∞x​(1+x)i−1​ui=1−u1−(1+x)​u\Phi(u)\;=\;1\,+\,\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}x(1+x)^{i-1}u^{i}\;=\;{1-u\over 1\,-\,(1+x)u} (4.28)

has a zero on the positive real axis at u=1u=1, which cannot happen for a Toeplitz-totally positive sequence [33, p. 412, Theorem 5.3]. However, by combining Proposition 4.5 with equation (1.26), we deduce that the generating polynomials of increasing ordered trees in ℐn{\mathcal{I}}_{n} with the weights ϕ{\bm{\phi}} are the second-order Stirling cycle polynomials c2,n​(x)c_{2,n}(x); and from Theorem 1.5 we see that the sequence c2,n​(x)c_{2,n}(x) is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx.

This example has an important consequence for the understanding of [37, Theorem 1.1] concerning the Hankel-total positivity of the generic Lah polynomials. We see that, although this sequence ϕ{\bm{\phi}} is not Toeplitz-totally positive, the resulting sequence of generating polynomials in [37, Theorem 1.1(c)] is still coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive. Thus, the condition of ϕ{\bm{\phi}} being Toeplitz-totally positive is only a sufficient condition and is far from necessary for the conclusion of [37, Theorem 1.1(c)] to hold. In [17], we take Φ⁡(u)\Phi(u) is to be a polynomial in uu of degree 33 or 44, and we study the exact necessary and sufficient conditions under which the conclusion of [37, Theorem 1.1(c)] holds true. ■\blacksquare

4.2.3 Vertex-marked increasing ordered trees

Having established Proposition 4.5, we are now ready to state our fourth interpretation for the second-order Stirling cycle numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}.

We define a vertex-marked increasing ordered tree to be an increasing ordered tree in which each leaf can be marked or unmarked; the internal vertices are always unmarked. For n=0n=0, we declare that the vertex 00 is always marked. We write ℐ^n,k\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{n,k} for the set of vertex-marked increasing ordered trees on the vertex set [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} with kk unmarked vertices. In this section we will show that the the cardinality of the set ℐ^n,k\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{n,k} is [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}.

Recall also from Section 4.1 that 𝒯^n,k\widehat{{\mathcal{T}}}_{n,k} denotes the set of trees in T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n} along with optional edge markings in which each edge can be either marked or unmarked such that left edges are always unmarked, and which contain kk unmarked edges.

Before providing the proofs, let us observe that using the bijection and the correspondence between left edges and internal vertices in Proposition 4.5, and we get the following corollary:

Corollary 4.14.

The sets 𝒯^n,k\widehat{{\mathcal{T}}}_{n,k} and ℐ^n,k\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{n,k} are in bijective correspondence. Thus, the cardinality of ℐ^n,k\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{n,k} is given by

|ℐ^n,k|=[nk](2).|\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{n,k}|\;=\;\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}\;. (4.29)

Proof. First notice that for n=0n=0, we have |𝒯^0,0|=|ℐ^0,0|=1|{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}_{0,0}|=|\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{0,0}|=1. Henceforth, we assume n≥1n\geq 1. For a tree S∈ℐnS\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}, let intvertex⁡(S){\rm intvertex}(S) denote the number of internal vertices of SS and let leaf⁡(S){\rm leaf}(S) denote the number of leaves of SS. Also, for a tree T∈𝒯′nT\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}, let l⁡(T){\rm l}(T), m⁡(T){\rm m}(T), r⁡(T){\rm r}(T) denote the number of left, middle and right edges of TT, respectively. Then we clearly obtain the following

∑k=0n|ℐ^n,k|xk=∑S∈ℐnxintvertex⁡(S)(1+x)leaf⁡(S)=∑T∈𝒯′nxl⁡(T)(1+x)m⁡(T)(1+x)r⁡(T)=∑k=0n|𝒯^n,k|xk\sum_{k=0}^{n}|\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{n,k}|\>x^{k}&=\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{I}}_{n}}x^{{\rm intvertex}(S)}\>(1+x)^{{\rm leaf}(S)}{}\\ =\sum_{T\in\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n}}x^{{\rm l}(T)}\>(1+x)^{{\rm m}(T)}\>(1+x)^{{\rm r}(T)}\qquad\qquad{}\\ =\sum_{k=0}^{n}|\widehat{{\mathcal{T}}}_{n,k}|\>x^{k}{} (4.30)

where () follows from the definition of the sets ℐn,ℐ^n,k{\mathcal{I}}_{n},\widehat{{\mathcal{I}}}_{n,k}, () follows from Proposition 4.5, and () follows from the definition of the sets 𝒯′n,𝒯^n,k\mathcal{T}^{\,{}^{\prime}}_{n},\widehat{{\mathcal{T}}}_{n,k}. This completes the proof. □\square

We thus have our fourth combinatorial interpretation for the numbers [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}.

4.3 Interpretation V: Cyclically-ordered phylogenetic trees

Here we introduce our fifth and final combinatorial interpretation of the second-order Stirling cycle numbers. This interpretation will lead us to a common generalization of the second-order Stirling numbers of both kinds and also lead us to another conjecture similar to Conjectures 1.3 and 1.4.

A phylogenetic tree is a leaf-labeled rooted tree (i.e. the leaves are labeled and the non-leaf vertices are unlabeled) in which all non-leaf vertices have at least two children. We refer to them as an unordered phylogenetic tree, an ordered phylogenetic tree, or a cyclically-ordered phylogenetic tree according to whether the children at each vertex are unordered, linearly ordered or cyclically ordered. Cyclically-ordered phylogenetic trees have also been called series-reduced mobiles [35, A032188] [1]. Let ℳn,k{\mathcal{M}}_{n,k} denote the set of all cyclically-ordered phylogenetic trees with n+1n+1 leaves and kk internal (i.e. non-leaf) vertices.

We will now establish the following proposition:

Proposition 4.15.

The cardinality of the set ℳn,k{\mathcal{M}}_{n,k} of cyclically-ordered phylogenetic trees with n+1n+1 leaves and kk internal vertices is given by

|ℳn,k|=[nk](2).\left|{\mathcal{M}}_{n,k}\right|\;=\;\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}. (4.31)

We will provide two different proofs of Proposition 4.31. Our first proof will show that the numbers |ℳn,k|\left|{\mathcal{M}}_{n,k}\right| satisfy the recurrence relation (1.15). Our second proof will use generating functions for the multivariate Ward polynomials introduced by Elvey Price and Sokal in [23].

Proof of Proposition 4.31 using recurrence relations. We will show that the numbers |ℳn,k|\left|{\mathcal{M}}_{n,k}\right| satisfy

|ℳn,k|=(n+k−1)​|ℳn−1,k−1|+(n+k−1)​|ℳn−1,k|.|{\mathcal{M}}_{n,k}|\;=\;(n+k-1)\,|{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k-1}|\>+\>(n+k-1)\,|{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k}|\;. (4.32)

To do this, we will consider two cases whether or not the leaf labeled n+1n+1 has exactly one sibling.

If n+1n+1 has at least two siblings, we can remove it, and the resulting tree belongs to ℳn−1,k{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k}. Conversely, to insert n+1n+1 into a tree belonging to ℳn−1,k{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k}, it suffices to choose the vertex that would be its immediately preceding (in the cyclic order) sibling in the resulting tree. There are n+k−1n+k-1 such choices. This contributes the term (n+k−1)​|ℳn−1,k|(n+k-1)\,|{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k}|.

If n+1n+1 has exactly one sibling, then the tree obtained by removing it is no longer a phylogenetic tree, as the parent of n+1n+1 would now have only one child. Instead, we proceed as follows:

  • •

    If the parent of n+1n+1 is not the root, we contract the edge between the parent and grandparent of n+1n+1 and then remove n+1n+1 from the resulting tree; this gives us a tree in ℳn−1,k−1{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k-1}. Conversely, to insert n+1n+1 back into this tree, we need to select an edge, and elongate it by adding an extra internal vertex and then insert n+1n+1 as the other child of this new internal vertex. As there are n+k−2n+k-2 edges, we get a contribution of (n+k−2)​|ℳn−1,k−1|(n+k-2)|{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k-1}|.

  • •

    If the parent of n+1n+1 is the root, we remove the root and the vertex n+1n+1 to obtain a tree rooted at the sibling of n+1n+1. Conversely, we can re-obtain the original tree by creating a new root whose children are the old root and vertex n+1n+1. This contributes |ℳn−1,k−1||{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k-1}|.

Putting these two contributions together gives (n+k−1)​|ℳn−1,k−1|(n+k-1)\,|{\mathcal{M}}_{n-1,k-1}|. □\square

For our second proof of Proposition 4.31, we require the multivariate Ward polynomials introduced in [23, pp. 9–11]. As mentioned in Section 1.3, our second-order Stirling subset polynomials s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x) are usually referred to as the Ward polynomials, and the numbers {nk}(2)\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)} are the Ward numbers. It is known [23, p. 5] that the Ward number {nk}(2)\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)} counts the number of phylogenetic trees (with unordered children) on n+1n+1 leaves and kk internal vertices. Thus, the polynomial s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x) is the generating polynomial of phylogenetic trees on n+1n+1 leaves in which each internal vertex gets a weight xx. Now let 𝐱=(xi)i≥1{\mathbf{x}}=(x_{i})_{i\geq 1} be an infinite collection of indeterminates. The multivariate Ward polynomials 𝑾n​(𝐱)=𝑾n​(x1,…,xn){\bm{W}}_{n}({\mathbf{x}})={\bm{W}}_{n}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) are a multivariate generalization of the polynomials s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x): they are the generating polynomial for phylogenetic trees on n+1n+1 labeled leaves in which each internal vertex with ii (≥2\geq 2) children gets a weight xi−1x_{i-1}. Thus s2,n​(x)=𝑾n​(x,…,x)s_{2,n}(x)={\bm{W}}_{n}(x,\ldots,x). The polynomial 𝑾n​(𝐱){\bm{W}}_{n}({\mathbf{x}}) is quasi-homogeneous of degree nn when xix_{i} is given weight ii. The first few 𝑾n{\bm{W}}_{n} are [35, A134685]

𝑾0=1​𝑾1=x1​𝑾2=3​x12+x2​𝑾3=15​x13+10​x1​x2+x3​𝑾4=105​x14+105​x12​x2+15​x1​x3+10​x22+x4{\bm{W}}_{0}&=1\\ {\bm{W}}_{1}=x_{1}\\ {\bm{W}}_{2}=3x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}\\ {\bm{W}}_{3}=15x_{1}^{3}+10x_{1}x_{2}+x_{3}\\ {\bm{W}}_{4}=105x_{1}^{4}+105x_{1}^{2}x_{2}+15x_{1}x_{3}+10x_{2}^{2}+x_{4} (4.33)

It is not difficult to show that the exponential generating function

𝒲⁡(t,𝐱)=def∑n=0∞𝑾n​(𝐱)​tn+1(n+1)!=t+∑n=2∞𝑾n−1​(𝐱)​tnn!{\mathcal{W}}(t;{\mathbf{x}})\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}{\bm{W}}_{n}({\mathbf{x}})\,{t^{n+1}\over(n+1)!}\;=\;t\,+\,\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}{\bm{W}}_{n-1}({\mathbf{x}})\,{t^{n}\over n!} (4.34)

satisfies the functional equation [23, eq. (1.18)]

𝒲⁡(t,𝐱)=t+∑j=2∞xj−1​𝒲​(t,𝐱)jj!,{\mathcal{W}}(t;{\mathbf{x}})\;=\;t\,+\,\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}x_{j-1}\,{{\mathcal{W}}(t;{\mathbf{x}})^{j}\over j!}\;, (4.35)

where the term jj in the sum corresponds to the case in which the root has jj children.

Proof of Proposition 4.31 using generating functions. With the specialization xi=i!​xx_{i}=i!\,x, the polynomials 𝑾n​(x,2​x,…,n!​x){\bm{W}}_{n}(x,2x,\ldots,n!\,x) are the generating polynomials of cyclically-ordered phylogenetic trees with weight xx given to each internal vertex and a weight 11 to each leaf. We therefore want to show that 𝑾n​(x,2​x,…,n!​x)=c2,n​(x){\bm{W}}_{n}(x,2x,\ldots,n!\,x)=c_{2,n}(x). We call these polynomials Wn​(x)=def𝑾n​(x,2​x,…,n!​x)W_{n}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}{\bm{W}}_{n}(x,2x,\ldots,n!\,x), and we denote the corresponding exponential generating function by 𝒲⁡(t,x){\mathcal{W}}(t;x). Thus, the functional equation (4.35) is now

𝒲⁡(t,x)=t+∑j=2∞𝒲​(t,x)j​xj.{\mathcal{W}}(t;x)\;=\;t\,+\,\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}{\mathcal{W}}(t;x)^{j}\,\dfrac{x}{j}\;. (4.36)

This can be rewritten as

𝒲⁡(t,x)=t−x​log⁡[1−𝒲⁡(t,x)]−x​𝒲​(t,x).{\mathcal{W}}(t;x)\;=\;t\>-\>x\,\log[1-{\mathcal{W}}(t;x)]\>-\>x\,{\mathcal{W}}(t;x)\;. (4.37)

Differentiating both sides with respect to tt and solving for 𝒲′{\mathcal{W}}^{\prime}, we obtain

𝒲′=11−x​𝒲1−𝒲= 1+x​𝒲1−(1+x)​𝒲.{\mathcal{W}}^{\prime}\;=\;\dfrac{1}{1-x\>\dfrac{{\mathcal{W}}}{1-{\mathcal{W}}}}\;=\;1+\dfrac{x\>{\mathcal{W}}}{1-(1+x)\>{\mathcal{W}}}\;. (4.38)

However, this is exactly the same as the differential equation (4.16) with y=1+xy=1+x which is satisfied by the exponential generating function for increasing ordered trees on [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} where each leaf is given a weight 11 and each vertex with i≥1i\geq 1 children is given a weight x​(1+x)i−1x(1+x)^{i-1}. Thus, the result follows by combining Proposition 4.5 and equation (1.26). □\square

Final remark and conjecture. As mentioned earlier, it was noticed in [23] that the number of phylogenetic trees with unordered children having n+1n+1 leaves and kk internal vertices is the second-order Stirling subset number {nk}(2)\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}. In Proposition 4.31 we established that the number of phylogenetic trees with cyclically-ordered children having n+1n+1 leaves and kk internal vertices is the second-order Stirling cycle number [nk](2)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(2)}. The generating polynomials in both cases can be obtained as specializations of the multivariate Ward polynomials: the former by setting xi=xx_{i}=x, the latter by setting xi=i!​xx_{i}=i!\,x. After these two observations, it is very natural to inquire about the number of phylogenetic trees with linearly-ordered children having n+1n+1 leaves and kk internal vertices. Let us denote this number by {nk}^\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}. Their generating polynomials are obtained by setting xi=(i+1)!​xx_{i}=(i+1)!\,x in the multivariate Ward polynomials. The first few of these numbers are

and they seem to match [35, A357367], namely1111 11 This explicit formula is not yet shown at [35, A357367].

{nk}^=(n+k)!k!​(n−1k−1).\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}\;=\;\dfrac{(n+k)!}{k!}\,\binom{n-1}{k-1}\;. (4.39)

This is, in fact, true:

Proposition 4.16.

The cardinality of the set of all phylogenetic trees with linearly ordered children having n+1n+1 leaves and kk internal vertices is given by (4.39).

Proof. We show that the numbers {nk}^\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}} satisfy the recurrence

{nk}^=(2​n+2​k−2)​{n−1k−1}^+(n+2​k−1)​{n−1k}^.\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}\;=\;(2n+2k-2)\,\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k-1}}\>+\>(n+2k-1)\,\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}}\;. (4.40)

Our argument is a modification of the proof of Proposition 4.31 using recurrence relations, and we leave the details to the reader. Equation (4.39) then follows, as it is easy to see that the numbers [(n+k)!/k!]​(n−1k−1)\big[(n+k)!/k!\big]\binom{n-1}{k-1} also satisfy the same recurrence. □\square

Let dn​(x)d_{n}(x) denote the generating polynomials

dn​(x)=def∑k=0n{nk}^​xk,d_{n}(x)\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\sum_{k=0}^{n}\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}x^{k}\;, (4.41)

and let DD be the lower-triangular matrix D=({nk}^)n,k≥0D=\left(\widehat{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}\right)_{n,k\geq 0}.

Similar to Conjectures 1.3 and 1.4, we have the following conjecture:

Conjecture 4.17 (Conjecture for ordered phylogenetic trees).

The following are true:

  1. (a)

    The triangle DD is totally positive.

  2. (b)

    The triangle DrevD^{\rm rev} formed by reversing the rows of DD is totally positive.

  3. (c)

    The sequence (dn​(x))n≥0(d_{n}(x))_{n\geq 0} is coefficientwise Hankel-totally positive in the variable xx.

The polynomials dn​(x)d_{n}(x) are also negative-real-rooted, and in this case we are able to prove it:

Theorem 4.18.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, the polynomials dn​(x)d_{n}(x) have 00 as a root; and the zeros of the polynomial sequence (dn​(x)/x)n≥1\big(d_{n}(x)/x\big)_{n\geq 1} are simple, interlacing, and lie in the interval (−1,0)(-1,0).

The proof of Theorem 4.18 is similar to that of Theorem 1.6 (which we will see in Section 6) and we omit it. ■\blacksquare

We leave the further study of the multivariate Ward polynomials as an open problem. In particular, it would be interesting to find sufficient conditions for Hankel-total positivity, analogous to [37, Theorem 1.1].

4.4 A final remark

The diagonal entries of the second-order Stirling cycle matrix C(2)C^{(2)} are (2​n−1)!!{(2n-1)!!} [cf. (1.12)], and the reader will observe that the first four of our combinatorial interpretations of the second-order Stirling cycle numbers are based on taking well-known [10] objects of cardinality (2​n−1)!!(2n-1)!! and then “augmenting” them:

  • •

    Perfect matchings of [2​n][2n] ⟶\longrightarrow Derangements of [n+k][n+k] containing kk cycles

  • •

    Stirling permutations of {1,1,2,2,…,n,n}\{1,1,2,2,\ldots,n,n\} ⟶\longrightarrow Ascent-marked Stirling permutations of {1,1,2,2,…,n,n}\{1,1,2,2,\ldots,n,n\}

  • •

    Increasing ternary trees on [n][n] ⟶\longrightarrow Edge-marked increasing ternary trees on [n][n]

  • •

    Increasing ordered trees on [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\} ⟶\longrightarrow Edge-marked increasing ordered trees on [n]∪{0}[n]\cup\{0\}

In fact, also the second-order Stirling subset matrix S(2)S^{(2)} has diagonal entries (2​n−1)!!(2n-1)!! [cf. again (1.12)], and the construction of Elvey Price and Sokal [23] was also based on a similar “augmentation”:

  • •

    Perfect matchings of [2​n][2n] ⟶\longrightarrow Augmented and super-augmented perfect matchings of [2​n][2n]

We wonder whether the rr-th order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials for r≥3r\geq 3 can be handled by a similar approach: namely, find a class of combinatorial objects enumerated by the numbers (1.10) or (1.11), and then “augment” them to handle the matrix elements with k<nk<n. We will use this approach to construct an analogue of Stirling permutations for r≥3r\geq 3 in Section 5; this will give us a new interpretaton for the rr-th order Stirling cycle numbers.

5 Interpretation for 𝒓\bm{r}-th order Stirling cycle numbers

We will now provide an interpretation for the rr-th order Stirling cycle numbers that generalizes the interpretation given for r=2r=2 in Section 3.2. We will also provide an interpretation for the rrth-order quasi-Eulerian cycle numbers ⟨⟨nk⟩⟩C(r)\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{\!(r)}_{\!\rm C}.

To begin, let us first provide an interpretation for the numbers [nn](r)=(r​n)!/(rn​n!)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(r)}=(rn)!/(r^{n}n!) for r≥2r\geq 2. To do this, let us first consider the multiset

Mn(r)=def{1a1,2a2,…,(r−1)​na(r−1)​n}M_{n}^{(r)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\{1^{a_{1}},2^{a_{2}},\ldots,(r-1)n^{a_{(r-1)n}}\} (5.1)

where aia_{i} is the multiplicity of the letter ii and it is defined by

ai={2if i≡0(modr−1)1otherwisea_{i}\;=\;\begin{cases}2\qquad\text{if $i\equiv 0\pmod{r-1}$}\\ 1\qquad\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (5.2)

Thus, for r=2r=2 we have Mn(2)={1,1,2,2,3,3,…,n,n}M_{n}^{(2)}=\{1,1,2,2,3,3,\ldots,n,n\} and for r=3r=3 we have Mn(3)={1,2,2,3,4,4,…,2​n−1,2​n,2​n}M_{n}^{(3)}=\{1,2,2,3,4,4,\ldots,2n-1,2n,2n\}. Let 𝔖n(r){\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)} denote the set of Stirling permutations of the multiset Mn(r)M_{n}^{(r)}. It immediately follows from [32, eq. (1)] that

[nn](r)=|𝔖n(r)|.\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(r)}\;=\;\left|{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)}\right|\,. (5.3)

The set 𝔖n(r){\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)} is our first ingredient. Notice that each σ∈𝔖n(r)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)} is a string of length r​nrn consisting of (r−1)​n(r-1)n distinct letters.

Our next ingredient is a new combinatorial statistic on Stirling permutations in 𝔖n(r){\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)}. Given σ∈𝔖n(r)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)}, we say that i∈[n]i\in[n] is a consecutive ascent in σ\sigma if the following two conditions hold:

  • •

    if the following r−1r-1 letters: (r−1)​i+1,(r−1)​i+2,…,(r−1)​i+(r−2)(r-1)i+1,(r-1)i+2,\ldots,(r-1)i+(r-2) and the first occurence of (r−1)​(i+1)(r-1)(i+1), occur consecutively in σ\sigma.

  • •

    the letter (r−1)​i+1(r-1)i+1 is preceeded by a lower-numbered letter in σ\sigma.

An alternate way of saying this is that the string a1​a2​…​ar−1a_{1}a_{2}\ldots a_{r-1} where aj=(r−1)​i+ja_{j}=(r-1)i+j occurs as a substring in σ\sigma and a1a_{1} is preceeded by a lower-numbered letter. Thus, if i∈[n]i\in[n] is a consecutive ascent in 𝔖n(r){\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)}, then the r−1r-1 letters, (r−1)​i+1,(r−1)​i+2,…,(r−1)​i+(r−2)(r-1)i+1,(r-1)i+2,\ldots,(r-1)i+(r-2) and the first occurence of (r−1)​(i+1)(r-1)(i+1), are the ends of ascents (i.e. aa in σi<σi+1=a\sigma_{i}<\sigma_{i+1}=a). Let CAsc⁡(σ)⊆[n]{\rm CAsc}(\sigma)\subseteq[n] denote the set of consecutive ascents in σ\sigma. We then define 𝔖n,k(r){\mathfrak{S}}_{n,k}^{(r)} to be the set of Stirling permutations in 𝔖n(r){\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)} with kk consecutive ascents:

𝔖n,k(r)=def{σ∈𝔖n(r):CAsc⁡(σ)=k}.{\mathfrak{S}}_{n,k}^{(r)}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\{\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)}\>\colon{\rm CAsc}(\sigma)=k\}\;. (5.4)

Notice that when r=2r=2, consecutive ascents are the same as ascents in Stirling permutations, so |𝔖n,k(2)|=⟨⟨nk⟩⟩|{\mathfrak{S}}_{n,k}^{(2)}|=\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle.

A consecutive-ascent-marked Stirling permutation of order 𝒓\bm{r} and size 𝒏\bm{n} with 𝒌\bm{k} dots is defined to be a pair (σ,D)(\sigma,D) where σ∈𝔖n(r)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{(r)} and D⊆CAsc⁡(σ)⊆[n]D\subseteq{\rm CAsc}(\sigma)\subseteq[n] and |D|=k|D|=k. We let 𝒱n,k(r){\mathcal{V}}_{n,k}^{(r)} denote the set of consecutive-ascent-marked Stirling permutation of order rr and size nn with kk dots. Thus, when r=2r=2 we have the interpretation in Section 3.2. For r=3r=3, we have 𝒱2,0(3){\mathcal{V}}_{2,0}^{(3)} is equivalent to 𝔖2(3){\mathfrak{S}}_{2}^{(3)} (as we always have D=∅D=\varnothing) which has cardinality 4040 and hence we refrain from listing out. For k=1k=1, we have

𝒱2,1(3)={122⋅3⋅44,12⋅3⋅442,1⋅3⋅4422}.{\mathcal{V}}_{2,1}^{(3)}\;=\;\{122\bm{\cdot}3\bm{\cdot}44,12\bm{\cdot}3\bm{\cdot}442,1\bm{\cdot}3\bm{\cdot}4422\}. (5.5)

Here we have inserted dots to the r−1=2r-1=2 ascents corresponding to each of the i∈Di\in D.

Let vn,k(r)=|𝒱n,k(r)|v_{n,k}^{(r)}=|{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k}^{(r)}| and bn,k(r)=|𝔖n,k(r)|b_{n,k}^{(r)}=|{\mathfrak{S}}_{n,k}^{(r)}|; then

vn,k(r)=∑i=knbn,i(r)​(ik).v_{n,k}^{(r)}\;=\;\sum_{i=k}^{n}b_{n,i}^{(r)}\>\binom{i}{k}\;. (5.6)

Notice that for r=2r=2, the identity an,k(2)=⟨⟨nk⟩⟩a_{n,k}^{(2)}=\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle together with Proposition 1.2(a), which gives us (3.4), implies vn,k(2)=[nn−k](2)v_{n,k}^{(2)}=\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-k}^{(2)}.

We will now establish the following lemma, which generalises Lemma 3.1:

Lemma 5.1.

The numbers vn,k(r)v_{n,k}^{(r)} satisfy the recurrence

vn,k(r)\displaystyle v_{n,k}^{(r)} =\displaystyle= (r−1)!​(r⁡(n−1)−(r−1)​(k−1)r−1)​vn−1,k(r)\displaystyle\;(r-1)!\binom{r(n-1)\,-\,(r-1)(k-1)}{r-1}\,v_{n-1,k}^{(r)} (5.7)
+[r⁡(n−1)−(r−1)​(k−1)]​vn−1,k−1(r)\displaystyle+\;\;[r(n-1)\,-\,(r-1)(k-1)]\,v_{n-1,k-1}^{(r)}

with initial conditions v0,kr=δk​0v_{0,k}^{r}=\delta_{k0} and vn,−1r=0v_{n,-1}^{r}=0.

Proof. Let (σ,D)∈𝒱n,k(r)(\sigma,D)\in{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k}^{(r)} be a consecutive-ascent-marked Stirling permutation of order rr and size nn with kk dots. Throughout this proof, we set aj=(r−1)​(n−1)+ja_{j}=(r-1)(n-1)+j where 1≤j≤r−11\leq j\leq r-1 and ar=(r−1)​na_{r}=(r-1)n.

First, notice that on deleting the r−2r-2 letters a1,…,ar−2a_{1},\ldots,a_{r-2} along with the two letters ar−1,ara_{r-1},a_{r} in σ\sigma together with n∈Dn\in D, if it exists, gives an element of 𝒱n−1,k(r){\mathcal{V}}_{n-1,k}^{(r)} if n∉Dn\not\in D, and an element of 𝒱n−1,k(r){\mathcal{V}}_{n-1,k}^{(r)} if n∈Dn\in D.

Conversely, to get an element (σ,D)∈𝒱n,k(r)(\sigma,D)\in{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k}^{(r)} with n∉Dn\not\in D from a one-size-smaller ascent-marked Stirling permutation, we insert the rr letters a1,…,ar−2,ar−1,ara_{1},\ldots,a_{r-2},\,\,a_{r-1},a_{r}. For convenience, let l=r⁡(n−1)−(r−1)​kl=r(n-1)-(r-1)k. Notice that there are l+1l+1 choices to insert the letter a1a_{1} (these consist of any of the r⁡(n−1)+1r(n-1)+1 spaces except for the (r−1)​k(r-1)k corresponding to dots), l+2l+2 to insert the letter a2a_{2}, and so on until we finally get l+(r−1)l+(r-1) choices for inserting ar−1​ara_{r-1}\,a_{r}. Thus, there are a total of (r−1)!​(l+r−1r−1)(r-1)!\binom{l+r-1}{r-1} choices.

In the other case, if (σ,D)∈𝒱n,k(r)(\sigma,D)\in{\mathcal{V}}_{n,k}^{(r)} with n∈Dn\in D, then the string a1​a2​…​ar−1a_{1}a_{2}\ldots a_{r-1} is a substring of σ\sigma. To get such a pair (σ,D)(\sigma,D), the string a1​a2​…​ar−1​ara_{1}a_{2}\ldots a_{r-1}a_{r} can be inserted into an element of 𝒱n−1,k−1(r){\mathcal{V}}_{n-1,k-1}^{(r)} in any of the r⁡(n−1)+1r(n-1)+1 spaces except the first space and those corresponding to a dot; thus, the number of choices is r⁡(n−1)−(r−1)​(k−1)r(n-1)-(r-1)(k-1).

This proves the recurrence (5.7). □\square

Finally, we use Lemma 5.1 to obtain our combinatorial interpretation for the rrth-order Stirling cycle numbers and for the rrth-order quasi-Eulerian cycle numbers; we state this in the following proposition:

Proposition 5.2.

The entries of the matrix QC(r)=C𝑤𝑖𝑑𝑒𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑐𝑘(r)​B−1Q_{\rm C}^{(r)}=\widecheck{C}^{(r)}B^{-1} of rrth-order quasi-Eulerian cycle numbers have the combinatorial interpretation

⟨⟨nk⟩⟩C(r)=|𝔖n,k(r)|.\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{\!(r)}_{\!\rm C}\;=\;|{\mathfrak{S}}_{n,k}^{(r)}|\;. (5.8)

Also, the rrth-order Stirling cycle number [nk](r)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)} counts the number of consecutive-ascent-marked Stirling permutations of order rr and size nn with n−kn-k dots, i.e., [nk](r)=|𝒱n,n−k(r)|\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}=|{\mathcal{V}}_{n,n-k}^{(r)}|.

Proof. We now need to show that [nk](r)=vn,n−k(r)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}=v_{n,n-k}^{(r)} and ⟨⟨nk⟩⟩C(r)=bn,k(r)\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{(r)}_{\!\rm C}=b_{n,k}^{(r)}.

From (5.7) it follows that the numbers un,k(r)=vn,n−k(r)u_{n,k}^{(r)}=v_{n,n-k}^{(r)} satisfies the recurrence (1.13) which is satisfied by the numbers [nk](r)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}. Since these numbers also satisfy the same initial conditions, we infer that [nk](r)=un,k(r)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}^{(r)}=u_{n,k}^{(r)}. Finally, from the definition of ⟨⟨nk⟩⟩C(r)\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{(r)}_{\!\rm C} and (5.6), it follows that ⟨⟨nk⟩⟩C(r)=bn,k(r)\left\langle\!\!\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}\!\!\right\rangle^{(r)}_{\!\rm C}=b_{n,k}^{(r)}. □\square

6 Location of zeros for the second-order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials

We will now prove Theorem 1.6 in this section.

For r,n≥1r,n\geq 1, it is clear from (1.17)/(1.18) that cr,n​(0)=sr,n​(0)=0c_{r,n}(0)=s_{r,n}(0)=0. Therefore, for n≥0n\geq 0 and r=2r=2 we define the polynomials c^n​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x) and s^n​(x)\widehat{s}_{n}(x) by

c^n​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{c}_{n}(x) =def\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}} c2,n+1​(x)x\displaystyle\dfrac{c_{2,n+1}(x)}{x}{} (6.1)
s^n​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{s}_{n}(x) =def\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}} s2,n+1​(x)x\displaystyle\dfrac{s_{2,n+1}(x)}{x}{} (6.2)

We will show that the polynomials c^n​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x) and s^n​(x)\widehat{s}_{n}(x) have simple and interlacing zeros in the interval (−1,0)(-1,0). To prove this, we will first obtain recurrences for the polynomials c^n​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x) and s^n​(x)\widehat{s}_{n}(x) and then evaluate them at x=0x=0 and at x=−1x=-1.

Lemma 6.1.
  • (a)

    The polynomials c^n​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x) satisfy the recurrence relation

    c^n​(x)=[(n+2)​x+n+1]​c^n−1​(x)+x⁡(x+1)​c^n−1′​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x)\;=\;\big[(n+2)x+n+1\big]\,\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x)\,+\,x(x+1)\,\widehat{c}_{n-1}^{\prime}(x) (6.3)
  • (b)

    The polynomials s^n​(x)\widehat{s}_{n}(x) satisfy the recurrence relation

    s^n​(x)=[(n+2)​x+1]​s^n−1​(x)+x⁡(x+1)​s^n−1′​(x)\widehat{s}_{n}(x)\;=\;\big[(n+2)x+1\big]\,\widehat{s}_{n-1}(x)\,+\,x(x+1)\,\widehat{s}_{n-1}^{\prime}(x) (6.4)

Proof. As a consequence of the recurrences (1.15)/(1.16), the polynomials c2,n​(x)c_{2,n}(x) and s2,n​(x)s_{2,n}(x) satisfy the recurrences

c2,n​(x)\displaystyle c_{2,n}(x) =\displaystyle= [n​x+(n−1)]​c2,n−1​(x)+x⁡(x+1)​c2,n−1′​(x)\displaystyle[nx+(n-1)]\,c_{2,n-1}(x)\,+\,x(x+1)\,c_{2,n-1}^{\prime}(x) (6.5)
s2,n​(x)\displaystyle s_{2,n}(x) =\displaystyle= n​x​s2,n−1​(x)+x⁡(x+1)​s2,n−1′​(x)\displaystyle nx\,s_{2,n-1}(x)\,+\,x(x+1)\,s_{2,n-1}^{\prime}(x) (6.6)

from which the recurrences (6.3)/(6.4) follow. □\square

Lemma 6.2.

For all n≥1n\geq 1, the polynomials c^n​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x) and s^n​(x)\widehat{s}_{n}(x) have the following calues at x=0x=0 and at x=−1x=-1:

c^n​(0)=(n+1)!​s^n​(0)=1​c^n​(−1)=(−1)n​s^n​(−1)=(−1)n​(n+1)!\widehat{c}_{n}(0)&=(n+1)!\\ \widehat{s}_{n}(0)=1\\ \widehat{c}_{n}(-1)=(-1)^{n}\\ \widehat{s}_{n}(-1)=(-1)^{n}\,(n+1)! (6.7)

Proof. These follow by substituting x=0x=0 and x=−1x=-1 in the recurrences (6.3) and (6.4) and then using induction. □\square

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.6.

Proof of Theorem 1.6. We prove it for the polynomial sequence c^2,n​(x)\widehat{c}_{2,n}(x). The proof for the polynomial sequence s^2,n​(x)\widehat{s}_{2,n}(x) is mostly the same and is left to the reader.

We first rewrite equation (6.3) as

c^n​(x)=x⁡((n+2)​c^n−1​(x)+(x+1)​c^n−1′​(x))+(n+1)​c^n−1​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x)\;=\;x\>\big((n+2)\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x)+(x+1)\widehat{c}_{n-1}^{\prime}(x)\big)\,+\,(n+1)\>\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x) (6.8)

Now, we use induction on nn. For the case n=0n=0, the polynomial p0​(x)=1p_{0}(x)=1 has no roots and hence the theorem is vacuously true. The case n=1n=1 can be checked to be true as well. Let us assume that the zeros of c^n−1​(x)\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x) are distinct and are contained in the interval (−1,0)(-1,0).

Now let pn​(x)=defGCD⁡(c^n−1​(x),(x+1)​c^n−1′​(x))p_{n}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}{\rm GCD}\left(\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x),(x+1)\widehat{c}_{n-1}^{\prime}(x)\right). By Rolle’s theorem, the zeros of c^n−1′​(x)\widehat{c}_{n-1}^{\prime}(x) interlace those of c^n−1​(x)\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x) and thus, lie in the interval (−1,0)(-1,0) and are simple. Thus we get pn​(x)=1p_{n}(x)=1. Thus, there are no common zeros between c^n−1​(x)\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x), c^n−1′​(x)\widehat{c}_{n-1}^{\prime}(x) and c^n​(x)\widehat{c}_{n}(x).

Now let −1<λn−1(n−1)<…<λ1(n−1)<0-1<\lambda_{n-1}^{(n-1)}<\ldots<\lambda_{1}^{(n-1)}<0 be the zeros of c^n−1​(x)\widehat{c}_{n-1}(x). We then have c^n−1′​(λj(n−1))>0\widehat{c}_{n-1}^{\prime}(\lambda_{j}^{(n-1)})>0 if jj is odd, and c^n−1′​(λj(n−1))<0\widehat{c}_{n-1}^{\prime}(\lambda_{j}^{(n-1)})<0 if jj is even. Hence,

sgn⁡(c^n​(λj(n−1)))=(−1)j.{\rm sgn}\Big(\widehat{c}_{n}(\lambda_{j}^{(n-1)})\Big)\;=\;(-1)^{j}\;. (6.9)

Furthermore, using Lemma 6.7, we also have c^n​(−1)=(−1)n\widehat{c}_{n}(-1)=(-1)^{n} and c^n​(0)=(n+1)!\widehat{c}_{n}(0)=(n+1)!. Thus, the proof of this theorem follows by using the intermediate value theorem. □\square

Let us finally conclude this section by mentioning that even though we have included a proof of Theorem 1.6 for the sake of completeness, one can obtain this result as an immediate consequence of a seminal result due to Liu and Wang [34].

7 Location of zeros for order 𝒓≥𝟑\bm{r\geq 3}

In this section we study the zeros of the rrth-order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials for r≥3r\geq 3.

7.1 Existence of nonreal roots for 𝒓≥𝟑\bm{r\geq 3}

Conjectures 1.3(c) and 1.4(c) assert that, for r≥3r\geq 3, the rrth-order Stirling cycle and subset polynomials are not negative-real-rooted. In this subsection we will prove this conjecture for the cycle case for all r≥3r\geq 3, and for the subset case for all r≥4r\geq 4. The subset case with r=3r=3 remains open.

We already know that cr,n​(0)=sr,n​(0)=0c_{r,n}(0)=s_{r,n}(0)=0 for n≥1n\geq 1. One sufficient condition to show that a polynomial p⁡(x)p(x) has non-real complex zeros is to show that the polynomial dmd​xm​p​(x)\dfrac{d^{m}}{dx^{m}}p(x) for some m≤deg⁡(p)m\leq{\rm deg}(p) has non-real complex zeros. In this section, we will show that the polynomials dn−3d​xn−3​(cr,n​(x)/x)\dfrac{d^{n-3}}{dx^{n-3}}(c_{r,n}(x)/x) and dn−3d​xn−3​(sr,n​(x)/x)\dfrac{d^{n-3}}{dx^{n-3}}(s_{r,n}(x)/x), which are quadratic polynomials, have a negative discriminant when r,n≥3r,n\geq 3 in the cycle case and r≥4r\geq 4, n≥3n\geq 3 in the subset case. This will prove that in these cases the polynomials cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x) and sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x) must have some complex non-real zeros. We will then provide plots for the distribution of these zeros which suggest that these zeros accumulate around some mysterious limiting curves.

We first notice that

dn−3d​xn−3​(cr,n​(x)/x)=(n−1)!2​[nn](r)​x2+(n−2)!​[nn−1](r)​x+(n−3)!​[nn−2]\dfrac{d^{n-3}}{dx^{n-3}}(c_{r,n}(x)/x)\;=\;\dfrac{(n-1)!}{2}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(r)}x^{2}\,+\,(n-2)!\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-1}^{(r)}x\,+\,(n-3)!\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-2} (7.1)

We have already seen in (1.10) that [nn](r)=(r​n)!/(rn​n!)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(r)}=(rn)!/(r^{n}n!). We now obtain the following exact expressions either by using the combinatorial descriptions or by the recurrences (1.13):

[nn−1](r)=(r⁡(n−1)+1)!(r+1)​rn−2​(n−2)!​[nn−2](r)=(r⁡(n−2)+2)!​(r⁡(r+2)​(n−1)+ 2)2​(r+1)2​(r+2)​rn−3​(n−3)!\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-1}^{(r)}&=\dfrac{(r(n-1)+1)!}{(r+1)r^{n-2}(n-2)!}\\ \genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-2}^{(r)}=\dfrac{(r(n-2)+2)!\;\bigl(r(r+2)(n-1)\,+\,2\bigr)}{2\,(r+1)^{2}\,(r+2)\,r^{n-3}\,(n-3)!} (7.2)

With this information, we prove the following proposition:

Proposition 7.1.

Let Dr​(n)D_{r}(n) be the discriminant of the quadratic polynomial
dn−3d​xn−3​(cr,n​(x)/x)\dfrac{d^{n-3}}{dx^{n-3}}(c_{r,n}(x)/x). For all r,n≥3r,n\geq 3, we have Dr​(n)<0D_{r}(n)<0.

Proof. From (7.1), we write out the exact expression for Dr​(n)D_{r}(n), which is

Dn(r)=((n−2)![nn−1](r))2− 2(n−1)!(n−3)![nn](r)[nn−2](r)=(r(n−1)+1)!2(r+1)2​r2​n−4−(r​n)!​(r⁡(n−2)+2)!​((r+2)​r​(n−1)+2)n⁡(r+2)​(r+1)2​r2​n−3=(r⁡(n−1)+1)!​(r⁡(n−2)+2)!(r+1)2​r2​n−4⋅((r⁡(n−1)+1)!(r⁡(n−2)+2)!−((r+2)​r​(n−1)+2)n⁡(r+2)​r⋅(r​n)!(r⁡(n−1)+1)!)=(r⁡(n−1)+1)!​(r⁡(n−2)+2)!(r+1)2​r2​n−4⋅((rn−(r−1))(rn−(r−1)−1)⋯(rn−2(r−1)+1)−((r+2)​r​(n−1)+2)n⁡(r+2)​r⋅(rn)(rn−1)⋯(rn−(r−1)+1))D_{n}(r)&=\left((n-2)!\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-1}^{(r)}\right)^{2}\,-\,2(n-1)!(n-3)!\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n}^{(r)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{n-2}^{(r)}\\ =\dfrac{(r(n-1)+1)!^{2}}{(r+1)^{2}r^{2n-4}}\\ \,-\,\dfrac{(rn)!(r(n-2)+2)!((r+2)r(n-1)+2)}{n(r+2)(r+1)^{2}r^{2n-3}}\\ =\dfrac{(r(n-1)+1)!(r(n-2)+2)!}{(r+1)^{2}r^{2n-4}}\cdot\left(\dfrac{(r(n-1)+1)!}{(r(n-2)+2)!}\right.\\ \,-\,\left.\dfrac{((r+2)r(n-1)+2)}{n(r+2)r}\cdot\dfrac{(rn)!}{(r(n-1)+1)!}\right)\\ =\dfrac{(r(n-1)+1)!(r(n-2)+2)!}{(r+1)^{2}r^{2n-4}}\cdot\\ \Biggl((rn-(r-1))(rn-(r-1)-1)\cdots(rn-2(r-1)+1)\\ \,-\,\dfrac{((r+2)r(n-1)+2)}{n(r+2)r}\cdot(rn)(rn-1)\cdots(rn-(r-1)+1)\Biggr) (7.3)

Notice that when r,n≥3r,n\geq 3, we have

(r​n−(r−1))​(r​n−(r−1)−1)−((r+2)​r​(n−1)+2)n⁡(r+2)​r⋅(r​n)​(r​n−1)=−n⁡(r3−2​r)+(r3−4​r+2)r+2<0.(rn-(r-1))(rn-(r-1)-1)-\dfrac{((r+2)r(n-1)+2)}{n(r+2)r}\cdot(rn)(rn-1)\\ =\;\dfrac{-n(r^{3}-2r)+(r^{3}-4r+2)}{r+2}<0\;. (7.4)

It is easy to compare the remaining terms and it follows that Dr​(n)<0D_{r}(n)<0 for r,n≥3r,n\geq 3. □\square

Corollary 7.2.

For r,n≥3r,n\geq 3, the polynomial cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x) has some nonreal zeros.

One can use a similar argument to show that the discriminant of the quadratic polynomial dn−3d​xn−3​(sr,n​(x)/x)\dfrac{d^{n-3}}{dx^{n-3}}(s_{r,n}(x)/x) is negative when r≥4r\geq 4 and n≥3n\geq 3; we leave the details to the reader. This implies:

Corollary 7.3.

For r≥4r\geq 4 and n≥3n\geq 3, the polynomial sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x) has some nonreal zeros.

For r=3r=3, computational evidence suggests that the zeros of dn−3d​xn−3​(s3,n​(x)/x)\dfrac{d^{n-3}}{dx^{n-3}}(s_{3,n}(x)/x) are real, but that the polynomials s3,n​(x)s_{3,n}(x) nevertheless have some non-real complex zeros for n≥4n\geq 4.

Let us first establish some notation before we provide the plots for the zeros of the polynomials cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x) and sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x). Let 𝒜⊂ℂ{\mathcal{A}}\subset\mathbb{C} be a subset of complex numbers, let α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} be a real number. We then define the set α​𝒜\alpha{\mathcal{A}} as follows:

α​𝒜=def{α​x:x∈𝒜}.\alpha\,{\mathcal{A}}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\;\{\alpha x\>:x\in{\mathcal{A}}\}\;. (7.5)

For a fixed r≥1r\geq 1, we let ℛ​𝒞r,n\mathcal{RC}_{r,n} and ℛ​𝒮r,n\mathcal{RS}_{r,n} denote the set of zeros of the rrth-order Stirling cycle polynomial cr,n​(x)c_{r,n}(x), and of the rrth-order Stirling subset polynomial sr,n​(x)s_{r,n}(x), respectively:

ℛ​𝒞r,n=def{z∈ℂ:cr,n​(z)=0}​ℛ​𝒮r,n=def{z∈ℂ:sr,n​(z)=0}.\mathcal{RC}_{r,n}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\{z\in\mathbb{C}\>\colon c_{r,n}(z)=0\}\\ \mathcal{RS}_{r,n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\{z\in\mathbb{C}\>\colon s_{r,n}(z)=0\}\;. (7.6)

In Sections 7.2 and 7.3, we provide normalised plots of ℛ​𝒞r,n\mathcal{RC}_{r,n} and ℛ​𝒮r,n\mathcal{RS}_{r,n}, respectively, for 3≤r≤103\leq r\leq 10. These plots will immediately suggest some problems and conjectures which we mention.

7.2 Stirling cycle polynomials of order 𝒓≥𝟑\bm{r\geq 3}

We fix rr and plot the set nr−2​ℛ​𝒞r,nn^{r-2}\mathcal{RC}_{r,n} for n=50,100,150,200n=50,100,150,200 using the different colors red, green, blue and black, respectively. The overlapping plots suggest that the zeros have some asymptotic distribution supported on some limiting curves. We plot the cases r=3,4,5,6r=3,4,5,6 in Figure 2 and r=7,8,9,10r=7,8,9,10 in Figure 3.

Our plots suggest the following problem:

Problem 7.4.

For a fixed r≥1r\geq 1, study the asymptotic distribution of the set of normalised zeros nr−2​ℛ​𝒞r,nn^{r-2}\,\mathcal{RC}_{r,n}. Do they accumulate on a curve? If so, what curve?

In the case r=1r=1, we clearly get that the normalised zeros accumulate uniformly on the unit interval [−1,0][-1,0].

When r=3r=3, we conjecture the following:

Conjecture 7.5.

The zeros of the third-order Stirling cycle polynomials c3,n​(x)c_{3,n}(x) lie on the left-half plane.

7.3 Stirling subset polynomials of order 𝒓≥𝟑\bm{r\geq 3}

We fix rr and plot the set nr−2​ℛ​𝒮r,nn^{r-2}\mathcal{RS}_{r,n} for n=50,100,150,200n=50,100,150,200 using the different colors red, green, blue and black, respectively. The overlapping plots suggest that the zeros have some asymptotic distribution supported on some limiting curves. We plot the cases r=3,4,5,6r=3,4,5,6 in Figure 4 and r=7,8,9,10r=7,8,9,10 in Figure 5.

Our plots suggest the following problem:

Problem 7.6.

For a fixed r≥1r\geq 1, study the asymptotic distribution of the set of normalised zeros nr−2​ℛ​𝒮r,nn^{r-2}\,\mathcal{RS}_{r,n}. Do they accumulate on a curve? If so, what curve?

In the case r=1r=1, the asymptotic distribution of the normalised zeros of the Bell polynomials — which lie on the negative real axis — was studied by Elbert [21, 22].

When r=3r=3, we conjecture the following:

Conjecture 7.7.

The zeros of the third-order Stirling subset polynomials s3,n​(x)s_{3,n}(x) lie on the left-half plane.

Appendix C Report on systematic verification of conjectures

We will now report the results of our systematic experiments, i.e., we will write out up to which order we have verified each of our conjectures.

Our total positivity tests were performed by using the following methods:

  • •

    For a finite matrix AA with real entries, an efficient method to test total positivity is by computing the bidiagonal factorization using Neville elimination [27]. We used this technique to test the total positivity of lower-triangular matrices.

  • •

    For checking negative-real-rootedness of polynomials, we used Mathematica’s built-in NSolve command to list out approximate values of the zeros. This method is very efficient.

  • •

    For checking coefficientwise Hankel-total posivity of a sequence of polynomials, we unfortunately have to compute and check all minors of the Hankel matrix. No other efficient method is known. Compared to the other two types of tests, this method is very slow and we can check this only for matrices of small sizes.

We now present the reports for Conjectures 1.3, 1.4, 1.8, 1.9, and 4.17.

Conjecture 1.3:

The order up to which the various conjectures in Conjecture 1.3 have been verified is recorded in Table 1. We have checked that Cwidecheck(r)\widecheck{C}^{(r)} is not totally positive for r≥3r\geq 3. For r=3r=3, the 6×66\times 6 top left submatrix fails to be totally positive. For r≥4r\geq 4, we in fact have a 2×22\times 2 minor which is negative; it is

[22](r)​[32](r)−[21](r)​[33](r).\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{2}{2}^{(r)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{3}{2}^{(r)}-\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{2}{1}^{(r)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{3}{3}^{(r)}\;. (C.1)

Conjecture 1.4:

The order up to which the various conjectures in Conjecture 1.4 have been verified is recorded in Table 2. We have checked that Swidecheck(r)\widecheck{S}^{(r)} is not totally positive for r≥3r\geq 3. For r=3r=3, the 13×1313\times 13 top left submatrix fails to be totally positive. For r≥4r\geq 4, we in fact have a 2×22\times 2 minor which is negative; it is

{22}(r)​{32}(r)−{21}(r)​{33}(r).\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{2}{2}^{(r)}\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{3}{2}^{(r)}-\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{2}{1}^{(r)}\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{3}{3}^{(r)}\;. (C.2)

For r≥3r\geq 3, the Hankel matrices (sr,n+k​(x))n,k≥0(s_{r,n+k}(x))_{n,k\geq 0} fail to be coefficientwise totally positive. In fact, it seems that for r≥3r\geq 3, the 3×33\times 3 minor |(sr,n+k​(x))1≤n≤3,0≤k≤2||(s_{r,n+k}(x))_{1\leq n\leq 3,0\leq k\leq 2}| is has some negative coefficients.

Conjectures 1.8 and 1.9:

Conjectures 1.8(b) and (b′) have been tested for r=2,…,10r=2,\ldots,10 for the 50×5050\times 50 leading principal submatrix. Conjecture 1.9 has been tested for r=3,…,10r=3,\ldots,10 for the 9×99\times 9 leading principal submatrix.
